en: Victorious is he who is born of desire, the bee that kisses the hundred-petaled lotus of Rati’s face—
he whose dwelling is the sidelong glance from the eyes of an enamored woman.

Disregarding the multitude of faults and fixing your minds upon this small measure of merit, O noble ladies, listen to this work composed by Dāmodaragupta according to the opinion of a *kuṭṭanī*. (DKuṭṭ_2)
Indeed, there exists a city named Vārāṇasī, which is an ornament for the entire earth, endowed with prosperity and virtues, and frequented by people devoted to disciplined practice. (DKuṭṭ_3)

Even for embodied beings who experience sensual enjoyments there according to their desire, it is said that dissolution into the body of the one adorned with a crescent moon is not difficult to attain. (DKuṭṭ 4)
In that city, even the courtesans— whose bodies were adorned with the moon, who delighted in sacred ash, and who were surrounded by noble serpents— attained a state equal to the body of Paśupati.
There, the sky shines as if covered in clusters of blossoms by the Vaijayantī banners, tossed by the wind rising from the peaks of the exceedingly lofty celestial mansions.
There, the surface of the earth bears a splendor like that of a land of lotuses, reddened by the liquid lac from the soles of the feet of women moving about incessantly.
And there, in that place where every quarter of the sky and atmosphere was deafened by the sound of the ornaments of beautiful women,
the teachers did not perceive any fault in their students as they recited.
She shines like the ground of the Vindhya mountain range, graced by rutting elephants;
and she is like the night of the full moon, adorned with brilliantly shining constellations.
She was endowed with the virtues of a multitude of ascetics, like a constant collection of Vedic meters;
she possessed sal trees like a forest grove, and was filled with many Gandharvas like the army of the Turuṣkas.
In that place, the host of stars is of low birth; the owls are constantly fond of faults;
there is a falling away from meter in prose; and likewise, there is the besieging of others' houses in gambling.
Wherein the wielder of the trident was a snake among those who know the sacred verses;
alchemy was practiced among the gods; the assault of women upon men occurred during sexual union; and the cutting off of the temples of elephants took place when their rut had ceased.
There, the sun’s rays are scorching, the hearts of friends lack discernment,
ascetics take up the rod of punishment, and the breaking of embankments occurs among those who should be cherished.
In the rules for the arrangement of meters, there is the presence of heavy syllables in improper positions;
on the lute, there is the sound of discordant strings; and in the dwellings of the twice-born, there is a lack of serenity.
In dramas composed by excellent poets, in worldly affairs,
in the speech of charming women, and in poetic compositions, there is sweetness in her through the crafting of appropriate meters.
In that grove path, the *tamāla* leaves are found upon the faces of young women;
the sound of fingernails scratching is heard in stringed instruments and in the tumult of amorous play.
Delightful like the Nandana grove, filled with wise men, and frequented by celestial nymphs—
that other city which was created in the world by the Creator of the universe is like Amarāvatī itself.
Like the body of the king of birds, she gave rise to grief in the hearts of the amorous;
like the daughter of the sovereign of the snowy mountains, she had captivated the heart of the Lord.
With eyes fixed upon their attached enjoyments, they were like the form of Mount Mandara,
or like the scratches upon the body of the blind Asura as it was impaled upon the tridents above.
There dwelt a courtesan named Mālatī, who was like the embodied power of the god of love, and the ornament of all the women of the city.
She is the abode of gentle speech, the home of playful charms, the seat of affection,
the ground of jests, and the dwelling place of clever, indirect talk.
Once, while she was atop the roof of her white palace, she heard this Āryā verse being sung by someone as it happened to fall within the course of their conversation.
Having cast far away the intoxication of youth and beauty,
courtesans must diligently learn the means of winning the hearts of lovers.
Having heard this, Mālatī, with her broad hips, reflected for a long time in her mind:
"What has been taught by this virtuous reciter is most timely, as if by a friend."
Therefore, let us go and ask Vikarālā, who has mastered the entire cycle of existence,
at whose doorway the throng of lustful people waits day and night.
Having thus resolved in her mind, she descended very quickly from the roof of the palace and,
surrounded by her attendants, proceeded toward the magnificent mansion of Vikarālā.
Then [he saw] one with widely spaced and protruding teeth, a sunken jaw, and a thick, flattened tip of the nose;
her body was emaciated and flaccid, with the area of her breasts marked by prominent nipples and shriveled bosoms.
With deep-set, reddish eyes, unadorned and with long earlobes,
her few tresses were pale white, and her long neck was covered with a network of prominent veins.
She wears a pair of white, washed garments; her neck-thread is adorned with various medicinal herbs and gems;
and she bears a slender golden ring upon the base of her finger.
He beheld Vikarālā seated upon a couch, surrounded by a throng of courtesans, her gaze fixed upon the offerings brought by those seeking her love.
Having looked at him and performed a prostration with her head touching the circle of the earth, she— after he had inquired after her welfare and offered her a seat— took her place.
Then Mālatī, having formed her hands into a hollowed cup and respectfully relinquished her seat, spoke these words to Vikarālā when she had found the opportunity.
You render Hari devoid of the Kaustubha gem, the Sun god Indra-less, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) himself penniless—whenever they fall within the range of your intellect.
(DKuṭṭ 33)
This very world of lustful people, having lost their wealth and now clothed in rags, speaks of the abundance of their intellect while eating in almshouses.
Having withdrawn all other activities, Dhanavarman, having surrendered his entire prosperity to the pair of feet of the Lord of the Narmadā, attained the state of being Her footstool.
That Nayadatta, the middle son of Sāgaradatta, who has been brought here,
delights Madanasenā by leaving his father’s house empty.
Narasiṃha, the son of the venerable Mañjarī, attains supreme satisfaction as he gently massages with both hands those feet offered to him in play. (DKuṭṭ 37)
Śubhadeva, the son of the initiated Bhavadeva,
though his wealth has been entirely exhausted and though he has been rebuked, does not leave the gateway of Kesarasena’s house.
That even other common women, having assailed a man filled with desire, leave him as nothing more than a mere rag—this is the result of your teachings. (DKuṭṭ 39)
Even those born of low lineage, devoid of virtues, afflicted by disease, and outcasts—
such men have been served by me as well, while I manifested the excellence of my passion.
O Mother, what shall we do under the influence of the perverse ways of the Creator?
We do not attain our desired goal, even by putting our own bodies on sale as merchandise.
Therefore, O Mother, show me favor and instruct me as well, a living being,
regarding the objects of enjoyment and the means of casting the net of the arrows of the God of Love upon their dress, gestures, and minds.
Having touched with her hand the back of Mālatī, who was speaking these words with love, the beautiful Vikarālā addressed the lovely-formed girl with charming speech.
O beautiful one, this mass of hair of yours, appearing like a column of smoke rising from the fire of a burning lamp, reduces those who long for you to the state of servants.
O slender-waisted one, this very [man], who is the locus for the play of your slightly arched eyebrows,
surpasses all steadfast men by means of his special glances made charming by a sweet smile.
This very radiance of your face,
having reached the path of hearing, will surely produce an exceeding longing for Rati’s lover in the minds of those who desire her.
This very row of teeth of yours, possessing a luster equal to the splendor of beautiful lightning,
intensely produces for men the agony of the burning of the God of Love.
O Līlāvatī, this very speech of yours, surpassing the song of the cuckoo,
is marvelous, like a perfected mantra for attracting all lovers without exception.
O lady of enjoyment, this expansive pair of breasts of yours is the very abode of the god whose banner is the makara;
it is the means to pleasure—any recourse to other methods is futile.
O fair-limbed one, to whom does this pair of arms of yours— not expansive, yet as beautiful as a lotus stalk and adorned with golden armlets— not produce passion?
This very Middle Country, skilled in executing the commands of Kandarpa,
brings even those who are physically robust to the tenth stage of love's affliction.
This very line of hair, bearing the beauty of the string of the bow born of desire,
brings you young men to distress with the wounds of Cupid’s arrows.
O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, this very broad hip of yours, as delightful as a slab of gold-ore stone, is the subduer of youths and the destroyer of ascetics and their vows.

"O beautiful one, tell me, whose heart is not captivated by this pair of your thighs, so enchanting and resembling the core of a plantain tree? To whom do they not provide relief from the burning heat of the fever of love? (DKuṭṭ 54)
Who indeed would not desire this pair of well-rounded calves— which possess the grace of golden creepers upon the wish-fulfilling tree of youth— for the attainment of the fruits of desire?
Whose mind does this pair of your lotus-feet not adorn— feet that have surpassed the crimson glow of the pomegranate and conquered the splendor of the land-lotus?
It puts the lordly elephant to shame and mocks the swan as it strides;
O playful one, this very gracefulness of yours churns the hearts of the young men.
If you still have curiosity, O slender-waisted one, lend your attention;
listen as I speak according to the full extent of my own intellectual power.
First, O fair-limbed one, if you desire abundant wealth that is within your reach, accept with great effort the son of the royal servant Bhaṭṭa.
O daughter, when the father is constantly stationed at the royal camp in a nearby village,
the son of a Bhaṭṭa, Cintāmaṇi, will certainly be drawn [to you] by the lord himself.
Listen, O lady of lovely smiles, to his assumption of disguise and his conduct,
and how he swiftly falls into the reach of the beloved one whose bow is made of fragrant flowers.
His hair was arranged in five-lobed topknots, each as thick as a small cluster; his ears hung down, and his rows of teeth were set together like a pair of shears placed upon them. (DKuṭṭ 62)
Adorned with rings on his fingers and a golden necklace around his neck,
he was clothed in garments slightly tinged with yellow by the saffron rubbed upon his limbs.
His neck was beautified by golden ornaments consisting of hanging flower garlands,
while his feet were adorned with *turuṣka*, *khuśśikā*, and other substances mixed with beeswax.
Her hair was bound with thick, multi-colored silk ribbons,
while in one ear she wore a cluster of petals and in the other a leaf of lead.
He wore a loincloth dyed tawny with saffron and filled with bright gold,
and around his neck he bore a garland of very thick glass beads.
Accompanied by one who carries a betel-box, whose hand and fingers are dyed red with *vṛścikarañja*, and upon whose palm the conch and discus are inscribed, you display the appearance of early youth.
In the midst of a vast arena filled with guildsmen, merchants,
actors, and gamblers, he sat upon a small wooden seat placed by the executioner.
He was attended by five or six men who were his dependents, who carried swords resting upon their laps, spoke improperly, and displayed great arrogance.

With the front portion of his body draped over the backs of servants who were most skillfully attending to him, and with his hands placed like leaves upon cheeks swollen from suppressed tears; DKuṭṭ_70 //
Disregarding the logical consequences, he with his eyebrows raised recites again and again,
his mind cultivated, verses consisting mostly of *gāthās* and *ślokas*, exactly as they were learned.
With his head swaying in wonder, striking those standing nearby out of the impulse of his emotion,
he interrupts the hearing of another's sublime speech with cries of "Alas!", "Woe!", and words of praise.
Having been told this in private by the king with anger, the father likewise spoke to the king;
thus did the monarch reveal his affection and trust to his father.
Whether ignorant of or knowing his skill in the arts of leaf-cutting, he constantly displays it in the assembly of people while holding a pair of scissors. (DKuṭṭ 74)
In the science of dramaturgy taught by Brahmā, as well as in singing and the playing of drums and other instruments,
the mastery of Bhaṭṭaputra surpasses that of Nārada and others.

Even Paraśurāma, when he goes before him, inevitably assumes the role of Bhārgava [a mere servant] in the matter of the treasures, the wonderful staff, the pearl-weapon, the sword, the cow, and the bonds.
In this treatise on love, he considers the ignorant Vātsyāyana to be an outsider far removed [from truth], and he counts Dattaka Ācārya and the Prince as being equal to beasts.
This [generosity] of the son of Rādhā mocks the virtue of renunciation of one who, even when entreated with effort, gives away his armor,
yet showers wealth without a second thought.
That a lion should display valor even toward a deer whose sole heart's desire is flight— such bravery on the part of a "son of a Bhaṭṭa" is a cause for shame.
There is indeed curiosity even in hunting, and victory over a moving target;
yet the son of a Bhaṭṭa does not play because of fear of the Bhaṭṭa, though it is quite evident.
Thus, filled with internal joy by the satisfaction born from the words of Rāmaṇikā spoken by his own servant, he says: "This man is indeed mocking me."
What is the firm resolve, what is the departure, and who is the auspicious dancer?
Who dances in the brothel with the performance prescribed by Kohala and Bharata?
"What are you like in the path of *laya*, and what are you like in the *bhāṇaka* composed by Dhavala?
What are you like in the *prekṣaṇaka* and so forth?"—thus does he diligently question the instructor of dance. (DKuṭṭ 83)
With a respectful heart, he takes from his neck a garland of *sumana* flowers and,
removing it along with the betel, gives it to the dancer at an inappropriate moment, as well as words of praise.
The grace of her limbs as they rest upon her shoulders, her turning to one side, her standing postures,
her physical purity, and her four-square symmetry— all these were fashioned by this very [grace].
With distinct emotional sentiments (*bhāva-rasa*), through the artistry of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya-bhaṅgī*), and with various graceful movements,
she surpasses even Rambhā— how much more so the rest of the world of mortal dancers?
Thus, when the interlude has ended, the actor whose mind is prepared describes the situation with great intensity— his throat choked with tears—
as he observes every single word and syllable.
"O Vatsa, Bhaṭṭatanaya generally possesses such dress and behavior;
we shall tell you how to cause him to fall into the snare of Love."
A messenger who is clever, confident, endowed with skill in knowing the minds of others, and adorned with indirect speech (vakrokti) should be diligently employed for that purpose. (DKuṭṭ 89)
Having approached her at the proper time and offered betel and flowers, he should address her thus, O beautiful one, with words that kindle the god of love: DKuṭṭ_90 //
Today, the accumulation of merit gathered over thousands of lifetimes has borne fruit for us,
O delighter of the eyes, since you have come within the range of our vision.
Like an actress through the diligent application of her training, the courtesan displays flattery, passion, affectionate anger, and the anguish born of grief at separation.
Whether she is advanced in years or possessed of youth, born of a low family or a noble lineage,
diseased or of robust constitution— both yogins and courtesans regard her with an equal mind.
Even a wife who has been excessively honored appears like a common courtesan to a man whose wealth is exhausted;
she casts her gaze with longing even at the mere garment he wears as he departs.
Thus, for men whose minds have been so firmly conditioned, it is altogether improper to speak in their presence of the physical pain caused by the arrows of love for courtesans.

It is only because my friend, consumed by wicked hope, has cast aside all sense of shame and the weight of her steadfastness without a second thought that she makes me speak; therefore, I shall tell you.
O beloved of women, the heart of Mālatī was first struck by the arrow of the flower-bowed god; you, however, were the last to come within the range of her vision.
For a moment her limbs are bristling with horripilation; for a moment she is in a state of intense burning pain;
for a moment trembling arises within her; and for a moment her body becomes moist with sweat.
Now manifesting laughter for a moment, now abandoning her composure with loud cries,
she weeps, sings, and again and again resorts to silence.
Tormented by the god of love, she falls repeatedly upon her couch, then onto the lap of her attendants, then upon the ground,
then upon a bed fashioned of young sprouts, then into the water, and again and again.
Like a buffalo smeared with mud, like a female swan surrounded by a circle of lotus stalks,
O fortunate one, she has become like a peahen who hates serpents.
For her, the fire of passion, the plantain tree, sandalwood paste, lotuses, water, pearl necklaces, camphor,
the moon, and the moonstone are of no avail for bringing about peace.
"Remove the camphor, keep the necklace far away, what is the use of lotuses?
Enough, enough with the lotus stalks, O friend!"—thus the young woman speaks day and night.
With her mental faculties aglow, she draws you near through her volitions and firmly embraces you; yet afterwards, by the pressure of her own arms, she falls into embarrassment.
The flower-scented breeze, the warbling of cuckoos, and the humming of swarms of bees—
this entire collection has been brought together by Fate itself for her destruction.
Protect this weak woman who has been brought to this state by the powerful god of love;
for the birth of those of noble origin serves to rescue others fallen into calamity.
Generally, those who possess true merit do not heed the words spoken by supplicants;
nevertheless, out of boldness, listen as I describe even a mere fraction of Mālatī’s virtues.
Surely, as he was twanging his bow, the pollen of its flowers fell;
gathering that up, the Creator fashioned this woman of slender waist with it.
By means of that [ornament] which is constantly clinging to it, he mocks the beauty of the Daughter of the Mountain,
since the half-body of his serpent-king ornament has not been reduced to a liquid state.
Near her forehead, she bears a mass of dark, curly, and spotless locks of hair, resembling the shadow of the face of Rāhu as it rests upon the crescent of the moon's orb.
O beloved of my heart, with what could the face of Mālatī be equated—whether it be a lotus of unstable beauty or the orb of the moon devoid of its playful charm? (DKuṭṭ 111)
Having wandered above his two eyes, the bee—its excellence indicated by its fragrance—alights upon the lotus of his ear; even worthlessness is appropriate at the right moment.
Since her lower lip, surpassing the luster of the bandhujīva flower, naturally possesses a rosy hue,
the application of red lac upon it is merely a playful ornament for her.
It is a marvel that her waist, though gripped by folds of skin, has become so slender;
or rather, the thinness ordained by fate cannot be removed even by great effort.
Let alone anything else; even her exceedingly broad hips, the abode of Love, would cause even the sage Kapila to lose his meditative composure were they to fall within the range of his vision.
Beholding the pair of thighs of that woman whose body was like a plantain tree— thighs resembling plantain stalks—
even Makaradhvaja (the God of Love) suddenly became the target for his own arrows.

O enchanting one, because she does not move— tired and languid from the weight of her hips— and because she remains still as her eyes do not wander, the Moon-born Lord [Śiva] maintains his vow of celibacy.
If, by some chance, the Slayer of Madhu should behold this entire essence of the Tamasa-arrow,
he would consider it to be a mere burden of worthlessness placed upon the breast of Lakshmi.
If she should somehow fall within the range of Hara’s vision, then,
having reached the side of his body other than the left, she would surely render the three worlds inauspicious.
I consider that beauty, created by the Creator as something entirely distinct from all other women, to be a mere coincidence, like the "crow and the palm fruit."
I believe that even the thousand eyes of the Lord of Heaven would be fruitless for one who does not behold her body, the abode of innate splendor.
Let the God of Love slacken his flowery bow and cast his arrows into the quiver as long as Mālatī,
the very essence of worldly existence, wanders upon this earth.
Whatever little has been breathed forth by Vātsyāyana, Madanodaya, Dattaka, the poet Viṭavṛtta, the princes, and others—that all dwells within the region of her heart. (DKuṭṭ 123)
In the *Bharata*, *Viśākhila*, *Dattila*, *Vṛkṣāyurveda*, and *Citrasūtra*; in the rules for leaf-cutting, in the art of painting, and in the treatises on book-making and cookery; (DKuṭṭ 124)
If even the Lord of Serpents were able with his thousand mouths to describe her skill in the art of playing musical instruments, in dance, and in song— DKuṭṭ_125 //
In private, Mālatī, her garments slipping and disarrayed from above due to her impetuosity,
falls upon those lacking merit, her mind longing for sexual union.
The cooing of that woman, mingled with the sound of her trembling bracelets as they clash in the impetuosity of the essence of passion,
reaches the path of the ear only for one of no small merit.
If, while being addressed in this manner, he remains indifferent amidst pleasant words, then he should be spoken to by the messenger who displays her anger.
Is this pride of good fortune, this arrogance born of youth, playfulness, and beauty,
such that you do not hold Mālatikā in high regard, even though she has come to you out of natural affection?
She who takes no account of those who are of noble birth, wealthy, learned in the scriptures, and submissive—she withers away for your sake; shame on this misplaced affection!
The digit of the moon, which dwells upon the head of Śambhu—though he possesses intense radiance—is now amidst much ash;
and yet that same digit delights in you, who are like a mere beast. It is for this reason that I am so emaciated.
What wonder is it that Mālatikā, having resorted to the khadira tree— which is crooked, tasteless, hard, difficult to grasp, and harsh— should now come within the range of speech?
Or rather, what indeed is the fault that a crow,
feeling abashed by its own inferiority, avoids even the succulent lotus stalk within its reach?
Do not feel any distress, O fortunate one, that you have been addressed so harshly by me;
for to young men, the rough words spoken by a friend regarding a passionate young woman are indeed an ornament.
As moonlight is to the moon, as the forest garland is to the enemy of the demon Kaṃsa,
so was the creeper-like bow of the flower-arrowed god to his beloved, the springtime.
May that fair-limbed Madalīlā, who is like the goddess Halinī with her playful intoxication and like a string of pearls with her pair of breasts, become even more delightful when united with you.
What more need be said? If you desire to place your foot upon young men, then quickly take this jewel among women, radiant with love, from your lap.
"O beautiful one, having heard those words, my passion has been awakened like that of a noble heir; you too should treat me with such courtesy once I have arrived at your own dwelling."
Upon seeing [the teacher] from afar, one should rise to meet him, bow down, offer one's own seat,
and fan his pair of feet with the hem of one's garment.
Having briefly and effortlessly revealed the regions of your armpits, belly, armpits, and breasts,
you shall quickly depart from the range of the lover's sight in an instant.
Then he was led into the dwelling chamber, furnished with couches, rich with the fragrance of flowers, incense, and lamps shining brightly, and made beautiful by a spread canopy.
O lady with heavy hips, having respectfully performed the descent and other rites for you,
one should diligently honor you with these specific words of praise.
Today our blessings have been fulfilled and our chosen deities are thoroughly pleased,
since he has adorned this dwelling with auspicious ornaments.
Alas! For the Flower-Arrowed God, who today unites [the lover] with a worthy recipient, the long-accumulated fatigue of drawing his bow has finally borne fruit.
Having placed her foot upon the heads of all the courtesans, may our dear child now raise up this banner of good fortune, the very embodiment of auspiciousness.
Daughters alone are to be praised; fie on this world that is satisfied with the birth of a son, since it is through such a relationship that sons-in-law like you are obtained!
Although those like you, who possess firm familiarity [with the world] and recognize virtue, do not require entreaty,
nevertheless, O delighter of my heart, I speak out of affection for my daughter.
Mālatī has been surrendered to you with spontaneous love;
therefore, act in such a way that this poor girl does not become a dwelling place for the sorrows born of your displeasure.
Wearing soft, washed, and perfumed garments and unrefined ornaments,
with the incense-stick fully consumed, you shall stand near your lover, O fair-limbed one.
Looking with affection, modesty, trepidation, and longing,
her body partially visible, she spoke words charming with rare and playful jests.
When the mother has departed and the dwelling place has been cleared of attendants,
one should for a moment act contrary to the desires of the lover who is making advances.
When he, with his mind fixed on the battle of passion, suddenly draws you forward,
will you not display a graceful affectation of resistance by contracting your limbs?
"O daughter, when the act of love has begun, with the passion of the mind and the genitals aroused in due order, you shall offer your limbs without hesitation and without artifice."
Whatever she desires to kill, whatever she wishes to bite, and whatever she intends to scratch upon her body—
all that must be removed with haste and brought close to her.
At the bite, there is a pained "huṃ" sound; at the crushing, various throaty moans;
at the scratching with nails, a whistling sound; and at the strikes, a loud clamor.
Exhaling short and labored breaths, with a body bristling with horripilation and every limb perspiring, you will increase the passion of men.
At the appropriate time, you should melodiously imitate, with your sweet warbling, the heart-felt cries of the cuckoo, the sparrow, the swan, the pigeon, and the horse.
"Do not, do not distress me so; release me for a moment, O merciless one, for I am unable [to endure it]"—thus should the lover be addressed by you in words faltering and indistinct.
Having clearly recognized his state as a lover, you will display compliance, favorability, resistance, boldness, and even feigned incapacity during sexual dalliances.
When the impulse of passion has reached its height, you will engage in conduct that is improper, vulgar, utterly abandoned by steadfastness,
and a proliferation of immodesty.
With the wounds from my nails unnoticed and your eyes closed, you will remain devoid of energy,
your limbs relaxed once the hero’s task is completed.
Instantly, at the moment of dispelling the delusion, you will produce a covering for the hips, a smile accompanied by bashfulness, and a gaze languid with exhaustion, all born of physical weakness.
When the sexual union has been completed, having touched water in a secluded place, having washed his hands and feet, and having sat for a moment on a seat after gathering up his hair; DKuṭṭ_163 //

"Having dressed in garments that have been worn [by another], and having ascended the bed while displaying affection—thus you shall speak to that lover, having impetuously and firmly embraced him by the neck. (DKuṭṭ 164)
O son of a Bhaṭṭa, your wife must surely be dear to you,
since the embrace of no other woman brings such complete satisfaction to one whose heart is devoted to her.
Her birth is fruitful; she alone is enviable among all women.
By her alone has Gaurī been honored, and by her has penance been practiced that brings about good fortune.
She alone is the sole abode of virtues; her lineage is always praiseworthy—she, the possessor of hundreds of auspicious qualities, whose hand was taken by you in marriage.
Let alone that virtuous woman, the ornament of both her lineages and of noble form,
who does not depart from you, just as Lakṣmī never leaves the heart of the Enemy of Naraka.
O handsome one, even those women upon whom you cast your lotus-like eyes merely out of curiosity truly cannot contain within their limbs the joy that overflows from them.
Even a slight favor from a lord generally makes those of small mind talkative;
therefore, with my heart set upon my own interest, I make this request of you.
Whether due to intense passion, youthfulness, fickleness, curiosity, or even aversion;
whether through the abundance of my own good fortune, the skill of the messenger, or her very nature; ||| DKuṭṭ_171 ||
This small portion of affection shown toward us is our means of livelihood;
do not cause any obstruction here by perceiving the conduct of courtesans otherwise.
By which affection, anger, guile, courtesy, straightforwardness, and modesty—these exist in them as well, brought forth by the nature of living beings. (DKuṭṭ 173)
For courtesans whose hearts are overwhelmed by an intense, sincere love that has arisen spontaneously,
and who cannot endure separation from their beloveds, their very lives are as worthless as blades of grass.
In this regard, listen to a wondrous narrative which I shall describe;
it is that which even today the banyan tree bears as its distinguishing mark because of its connection thereto.
There is a great city named Pāṭaliputra, an ornament upon the surface of the earth and the ancestral home of the Sarasvatī, which surpasses the abode of Indra.
It was as if fashioned by Viśvakarman like a preliminary sketch to demonstrate his own craftsmanship to Viriñca, who was inquiring after his skill in constructing the city of the three worlds.
It is not resorted to by those seeking what is not beneficial; it is not overcome by the defect of being overwhelmed;
it is not claimed as its own by calamities; and it is untainted by the impurities of the Kali age.
The netherworld was filled with serpents; the ocean with masses of water and jewels;
the abode of the gods with hosts of deities; and the city of Kubera with heaps of wealth.
With beautiful women, it is the subterranean cave of the Asuras; with celestial musicians, it is the foothills of the Golden Mountain;
with sacrificial posts, it is the city of Hari; and with the power of tranquility, it is the abode of the sages.
Let alone the Brahmins whose stainless intellects have scrutinized all the scriptures;
even women serve as the touchstone for determining the quality of good and evil in that [work].
In that place, even though he remains hidden, he is inferred by his deeds— he who, out of fear of the rising Kali age, has clothed himself in the shawl of smoke from the sacrificial fires.
There, at night, the moon extends its rays as if to conceal its own blemish,
while the loveliness of the women flows forth from the buds of their faces.
In that [city], the canopy of its own bodily splendor, which dispels the mass of women going to meet their lovers and which darkens the sky like a veil of cataracts,
serves to interrupt their union with their beloveds.
Where, wounded by the sharp arrows of the glances from the corners of the eyes of women with shapely hips,
the world of travelers relaxes its longing for union with their own wives.
And where noble women possess a scarcity of speech, yet abundance in their hands and feet;
and possess clarity in their intentions, yet restlessness in their large eyes.
There is fullness in the weight of her plump breasts, natural passion in the lord of her life,
the beauty of folds in the rite of worshiping the family deity, and [such] beauty in the region of her waist.
Profundity resides in her natural disposition, in the navel that serves as the quiver for the arrows of the mind, and in the hips;
while expansiveness resides in her buttocks and in her heart, which is devoted to honoring her elders.
In that place, the amorous gestures of young women consist of the eyes acting like those of a deer, the closing of the lotuses (eyes),
and the curling of the rows of their hair.
In that [city], the restraint of the senses was a means of warding off the darkness of disease;
and the stiffness of the *sāla* trees was like a string of pearls joined with dangling gems.
In that place where serpents, watching for the vulnerabilities of others, bite the lips of beloved women,
those engaged in the practice of dancing experience the pain of needle-stiches.

In that place, even women whose bodies were bent, who were exceedingly straightforward, whose gait was slow, who delighted in their elders and the scriptures, and who were naturally innocent, became like the Narmadā river.
In that place lived one named Purandara, a preeminent among the twice-born who was purified by a hundred sacrifices; he was like Indra, a treasury of knowledge, and like a spiritual teacher.
The truthfulness of the son of Dharma, the enemy of Tripura—
who had constantly conquered the flower-bowed god of love— mocked the self-control of the one born from the navel-lotus of Hari.
Whether he was called "the one who humiliated Śiva," "the beggar" by the wearer of the Kaustubha gem,
or "the one who oppressed the son of the Earth" (Yayāti), no one showed him great respect during the time of Kāpila.

He who is greedy for following the path, who is averse to the destruction of living beings even while possessing a body, and who, though avoiding the wives of others, is delighted by the women of his own elders; // DKuṭṭ_196 //
In whose most noble lineage— like a lake, the natural abode of all living beings,
the birthplace of virtuous conduct, and the place where the spread of the impurities of the Kali age has been warded off— [he was born].
The taking up of the sword during the occasion of the libations to the ancestors was not out of pride in valor;
the breaking of the waist-bands occurred among the young men, not from the friction of passion in combat.
Our dispute regarding the differences in the Vedic recensions was not caused by a lack of division over inheritance;
rather, it arose because of their brilliance toward the sacrificial fire, not because of a desire for peace among these gods upon earth.

Stumbling occurs only for those who are old; the quivering of the lower lip only for those who are reciting prayers; a desire for sacrificial fuel only for those performing sacrifices; and contact with blackness only on the deerskin. (DKuṭṭ 200)
To him, whose two wings were illuminated by every art, there was born an only son named Sundarasena, like Kaca to the Lord of Speech.
Perceiving that embodied being to have been reduced to ashes by the fire from the eye of Paśupati,
the Creator fashioned him for the delight of Rati like another flower-bowed god of love.
Let alone other women of noble family; even that beloved wife of the Great Sage, upon beholding his form, preserved her conduct only with great difficulty.
Beholding his exceedingly broad chest, which bore the splendor of a plate of refined gold,
Lakṣmī thought for a long time that her dwelling upon the heart of Hari was unstable.

"How could such a thing be made if it were not fashioned from crescents of the moon? And if it were so made, how could it cause such pain?"—thus observing, the assembly of amorous women reached no certain conclusion.
He who took from the moon its pleasing form, from the mountain its steadfastness,
from the cloud its loftiness, and from the lord of aquatic creatures its profundity.
He who is the dwelling place of discipline, the refuge of cleverness, the station of steadfastness,
the abode of pleasant speech, and the home of virtuous conduct.
He who is the intoxicant for women, the moon for the lotus-cluster of virtuous men,
the touchstone for qualities, and the roadside tree for the world of travelers.
Devoted to the assemblies of the virtuous, he is a touchstone for the essence of poetry and prose;
he is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek his favor, and a playground for the goddess Lakṣmī.
Like the ocean to the moon, he shared in its growth and decline;
his friend was named Guṇapālita, who was purified by every test of integrity.

Once, while standing with him in private, he suddenly heard this noble verse being sung by someone in passing: DKuṭṭ_211: "He who, having seen a woman, does not desire her, and who, having desired her, does not enjoy her, and who, having enjoyed her, does not remember her—he alone is a man; others are merely the vessels of semen."
Those who do not understand the dress, customs, and speech in other lands,
and who do not attend upon their teachers, are oxen lacking horns.
Having heard that, Sundara spoke these words to his chief friend:
"This song is excellent, Guṇapālita; it has been well sung by this virtuous man."
The conduct of the virtuous, the behavior of the wicked, the various worldly fashions, the jests devised by the clever, and the indirect speech of unchaste women; DKuṭṭ_214 //
A man who wanders about comes to know the discussions of profound secret scriptures, the conduct of libertines, the methods of swindlers' deception, and the earth with its oceanic moat.

Therefore, my friend, casting aside this mere fragment of happiness found in the householder's life— which results in various kinds of gain— set your heart, together with me, upon the undertaking of departure.
To Sundarasena, who had spoken thus with a soul longing for the recovery of his friend, his companion spoke these words as if feeling ashamed: DKuṭṭ_217 //
The persistence of this request is indeed a cause for shame for those like me;
nevertheless, listen as we describe the sufferings of travelers.
His body covered with rags, his strength exhausted by the fatigue of a long journey,
greyed by clouds of dust, he longs for shelter at the close of day.
"O mother, O sister, have mercy! Do not be so cruel;
for even your own brothers and sons must depart from their homes due to the demands of duty."
Shall we uproot ourselves and go home tomorrow morning? Such is the dwelling of the virtuous, wherein travelers find rest as if it were their own.
"O Mother, let us somehow pass this night under your protection;
the sun has set—tell me, where shall we go now? (DKuṭṭ 222)
Thus, uttering many kinds of piteous words as he stands at the doorways of every house, the wretched man is reviled by the householders' wives who speak as follows: [DKuṭṭ 223]
"The householder is not here; why do you cry out in vain? Go to the temple! Even when told this, he does not leave—behold the obstinacy of a human being!
Then, if by some chance the master of the house, though repeatedly entreated,
points with disdain toward a corner of a dilapidated dwelling, saying, "Sleep here," ||| DKuṭṭ_225 ||
There, during the third watch of the night, the housewife remained quarreling with her husband, asking, "Why was this garment given by you to a stranger? (DKuṭṭ 226)
"O sister, what are you doing with this simple-minded man as your husband? You must remain vigilant in the house; indeed, such deceivers wander about in this manner."
Having thus formed the intention to beg for a vessel and other such items, a woman approached from a nearby house and spoke to her with a sense of intimacy.
Having wandered through more than a hundred houses, a traveler tormented by hunger eats as alms the rice, kulattha beans, millet, chickpeas, lentils, and so forth, all gathered together. (DKuṭṭ 229)
Fate has ordained for the traveler food dependent on others, the earth as his bed, and a temple as his dwelling; even a fragment of brick serves him as a pillow.
When he had thus spoken, and while it was Sundarasena’s turn to reply, this song was sung by someone in the course of conversation: *DKuṭṭ_231*

For those men whose minds are solely intent on their desired goal, even their own excellent palace is but a celestial abode, the earth’s surface is a most enchanting bed, and coarse food is nectar. (DKuṭṭ 232)
Having heard this from his friend, the son of Purandara, being well-pleased, said:
"This very thing has been made manifest by him as it was already in my heart; let it be so, let us go."
Then Sundarasena, accompanied by his companion and with his mind set on crossing the ocean of afflictions,
departed from Kusumapura without his father’s knowledge.
Visiting learned assemblies, practicing all the various weapons, comprehending the meanings of the scriptures, and observing diverse curiosities; DKuṭṭ_235 //

Knowing leaf-cutting, painting, the craft of wax modeling, and dance augmented by song, as well as the various types of stringed and percussion instruments such as the lute and the drum; // DKuṭṭ_236 //
Perceiving the deceptive maneuvers of rogues and the crooked speech of the jests of profligates and unchaste women,
Sundarasena wandered over the entire earth accompanied by his friends.
Then, having mastered all the sciences and understood the conduct of all people, he,
desiring to go to his own home, reached Mount Arbuda.
Perceiving that Sundara was intensely eager to see the region behind him,
Guṇapālita said, "Behold the king of mountains!"
This son of the Snowy Mountain, endowed with cool and clear waters flowing from its slopes,
was placed in the desert as if out of compassion for the world.

This mountain, with its crest adorned by the cool-rayed moon, where the wind-eater (the serpent) dwells as a girdle, and which is frequented by Guha, is served by the Vidyādharas; it bears the splendor of Śambhu.
Having formed the conviction that "these are flowers clinging to the tops of trees," I believe that at night a group of charming young women desires to gather the stars.
It is a marvel that even the seven sages stand at his side;
or rather, whom does the exaltedness of the great not attract?
Having perceived that the path of the sky is without support for the horses of the sun,
I believe this mountain was created by the Creator for their rest.
Relying upon this moon, the medicinal herbs have come into its proximity;
for proximity generally arises through the power of the benefactor.

As if to sprinkle them, this mountain releases streams of water droplets from its cascades for the elephants who are exhausted by supporting the earth; for there is indeed friendship among those who share a common task.
With its beauty enhanced by the presence of hārīta birds, joyful with parrots, delightful through the yoga of Vyāsa,
and where Bharadvāja has found rest— such is the abode of the Sage, which partakes in equanimity.
In this world, even those who are unattached exert effort toward the means of attaining the next world;
even those who feed on the wind are not harmful; and even those who eat fruit are not monkeys.
Even those who delight solely in auspicious deeds, who perform the six duties, who are self-restrained, independent,
and whose conduct is not fierce as they dislike it— even such devotees of Śiva dwell here, devoted to tranquility.
Like the form of the moon, it was graced by the *hariṇavatī* creeper and adorned with seven-leafed trees;
like the path of the sun, it was filled with foliage; and like the wife of a demon, it was possessed of a *palāśinī* tree.
Like a woman longing for her lover, full of passion, adorned with a forehead mark while preparing for her tryst,
the ground before the king’s gate was graced by Dhava, Hari, and Pīlu trees.
Covered by the multitudes of Arjuna’s arrows, the army of the Kuru lord appeared like the splendor of the sky’s expanse,
thick with thousands of stars.
Like the army of the Dānavas presided over by Riṣṭaka, this delightful grove shines like the night of the third watch,
illuminated by the rising Rohiṇī.
Thus he showed; and while his friend and Sundarasena were looking on with affection, this song, which had arrived at its proper occasion, was sung by someone.
Those who do not behold the back of Arbuda, which surpasses the very heights of heaven—
I consider their wandering through many realms to be for nothing but affliction.
Having heard this, he said: "Friend, what has been sung by this great-souled one is fitting; let us ascend and behold the beautiful peak of the mountain."
Then, having ascended the excellent mountain, he wandered about in wonder, gazing upon the various abodes of the gods,
the ponds, the garden lands, the lakes, and the rivers.
Like the newly risen sun freed from clouds, like moonlight deprived of its friend the moon,
like Rati abandoned by the God of Love, or like the Goddess Śrī fallen from the chest of Hari.
The collection of the Creator’s hands, the essence of all living beings,
the paragon of all beautiful things, and the victorious weapon of the God born of thought.
She is the abundance of blossoming flowers, the unique swan on the river of the erotic sentiment,
the creeper with playful sprouts, and the spear for those whose armor is mindfulness.
While wandering upon the surface of the earth, which was delightful with heaps of flowers in the groves and pavilions of the gardens,
he beheld a beautiful woman sporting together with her female companion.
As he gazed upon her, who had become a target for the arrows of the God of Love,
his mind was long overwhelmed by a weight of wonder.
Where indeed has this most wonderful skill of the Creator arisen, by which even these contradictory things have been joined together in a single place? For such is this [body].
Her body is graceful and faultless, delightful with shimmering, radiant stars;
her lotus-face is beyond description, and her speech surpasses the resonance of the lute.
Her bodily form is well-proportioned, her joints are joined with exquisite craftsmanship,
she is endowed with full and elevated breasts, and she is as radiant as the rays of the autumnal moon.
She dwells in the desired state of Sugata, her arrangement of feet is joyfully praised;
she possesses exceedingly broad hips, and she has brought forth beauty even from a shattered body.
Then, as his passion became manifest, that fawn-eyed woman, her eyes rolling,
suddenly fell into the power of the Flower-Arrowed God.
As she took refuge at the foot of the tree, having forgotten all other activities,
the creeper-like body of that woman suddenly sprouted the shoots of the sattvika emotions.
At that very moment, remembering Smara, that abundance of the grove began to afflict her;
for indeed, everyone performs the task of their master.
From her limbs, which served as fuel for the fire of passion burning within, perspiration issued forth like water from wood being consumed by flames.
Falling repeatedly into the net of the flower-arrowed god's shafts and turning her glances again and again,
that slender woman, gazing with unblinking eyes, imitated the female fish.
The god of love rendered her body rigid, trembling, bristling with horripilation, perspiring, and sighing;
for a rogue sports when he has encountered a superior object.
The swelling of her pair of breasts with sighs, the excellence of her graceful movements,
and the heart-stealing tenderness of her eyes through her longed-for love.
By causing her facial luster to shine with passion and her gait to falter with trepidation,
Love brought about an even greater beauty in her.
Even though her beloved was at her side and she was being struck by the shower of Kama’s arrows,
she was unable to speak the thoughts in her heart, fearing a breach of their affection.

Then, having discerned her state of mind, her friend drew her gaze away from her beloved and, laughing brightly, spoke to her as she was being consumed by passion: DKuṭṭ_276: "Then, having discerned her state of mind, her friend drew her gaze away from her beloved and, laughing brightly, spoke to her as she was being consumed by passion:"
O Hāralatā, cease this agitation caused by the burning of your body by Hara’s *huṃ*-utterance;
for true affection born of genuine feeling is not a commodity for courtesans.
Disregard the man destitute of wealth; show respect to those whose prosperity is not meager.
For for people like us, O charming girl, our very form was fashioned for the attainment of riches.
O slender-waisted one, by fixing your attachment on what is merely pleasant and disregarding the acquisition of wealth,
you are ridiculed by the ranks of clever courtesans.
For those whose youth is praiseworthy, for whom destiny has become favorable, for whom their past merits have borne fruit, and for whom there is a desire for the happiness of life; DKuṭṭ_280 //
Pierced by the arrows of Love, they will surely pursue you of their own accord;
for, O beautiful one, those who lick honey do not seek out mango blossoms.
When Ālī had spoken thus, Hāralatā— her entire body pierced by the shower of Kāma’s arrows—
spoke with difficulty, her syllables indistinct and faltering.
"Friend, first exert yourself in providing a remedy for this great suffering;
for those who are overwhelmed by calamity are not fit to receive instruction."
A beloved breeze not dependent on horses, fragrant flowers, and a garden—
this much indeed is the collection of things that belongs only to those whose lifespan has been exhausted.
Perceiving Ālī to have her body overwhelmed by the force of the poison of the serpent of passion,
the son of Indra approached her and, having offered his salutation, spoke with Śaśiprabhā.

Even if she restrains her speech out of embarrassment arising from her status as a courtesan, it must nevertheless be told; for in the case of a friend's misfortune, propriety is not to be scrutinized.
In this vast cycle of existence, those truly well-born are indeed counted as few—
those who flash forth in the minds of those whose hearts are distressed by calamities.
From the very moment you came within the range of my friend's sight,
she has fallen under the sway of the scorched Madana.
The arrows released from the bow of her mind-born [Cupid] have fallen upon her inner body, piercing through the armor of her bristling hair.
What can that poor woman do? Where can she find solace? To whom can she go for refuge, when even the ever-pure, gentle, and southern breeze torments her so intensely?
When her voice has become faltering, the cuckoos, having long since abandoned their vow of silence, are delighted;
finding their opportunity, they distress her friend with unrestrained cries.

As the slender-limbed woman’s gait becomes faltering and agitated, the swans— disregarding their own fatigue and having finally found an opportunity after a long time— joyfully perform their coming and going.
Even while being scorched by her hot sighs, the bee does not abandon the flower in her tresses; for sense objects are difficult to relinquish even in times of distress.
The humming of the honeybee, nestled among the flowers that fill her ears, seems to whisper into the ear of her, whose body is now frail, "Do not restrain me thus at this moment."
In that golden bracelet, which fell from her loosened vine-like arm to reach the earth,
"open-handedness" (liberality) was indeed the cause.
It is a marvel that it fell from her hips all at once, even though held by the quality of her girdle;
or rather, it was surely the natural course for one who serves a heavy wife.

Though he was cherished upon her breast after she had accepted his love, that wretched necklace tormented her friend at that very moment; for how can there be well-being from that which is internally divided?
The sweat-moisture, white with the [saffron] garment and mixed with tears as dark as collyrium,
falling upon the slope of her breast, resembles the waters at the confluence of the Prayāga.
Surrounded by cuckoos' cries, Malaya breezes, flowers, Cupid, and bees, this young woman— lusting for the bliss of an embrace with you— performs the "five-fire" penance.
This poor girl has not yet reached the tenth stage of love's passion;
O fortunate one, protect her meanwhile! For it is the great vow of the noble to protect those who have come for refuge.
Then, perceiving that his friend’s mind had been stirred by passion after he had shown respect for those words, Guṇapālita, his heart fearful of public reproach, said to his companion: DKuṭṭ_301 //
Although the influence of Māra is difficult to resist for living beings in their youth,
those possessed of discernment must nevertheless consider the ultimate end of the affection of courtesans.
The coquettish gestures, passion, love, longing, and the pangs of desire of courtesans increase and diminish along with [their own] prosperity; they are renowned as their wealth and their friends.

How could one of pure birth enter into intimacy with those women, who—though seen for but a moment, though full of affection, and though never before encountered in this life—remain strangers? (DKuṭṭ 304)
To the courtesans, Pradyumna is indeed Pradyumna, Virūpaka is truly Virūpaka, Susnigdha is always Susnigdha, and Rūkṣa is indeed Rūkṣa. (DKuṭṭ 305)
The covering of their hips was for the sake of increasing the curiosity of others, not out of modesty;
their arrangement of brilliant attire was for the attraction of those filled with desire, not for the sake of stability.
The consumption of meat broth is due to the distress of killing men, not out of desire;
addiction to painting and such arts is for the sake of proclaiming one's cleverness, not for amusement.

Passion resides in the lower lip and not in the mind; straightforwardness is found in the vine-like arms and not in one's nature; loftiness is in the weight of the breasts and not in conduct praised by the wicked.
They possess heaviness in their hips, not in noble families;
they exhibit sluggishness in the act of walking, not in the practice of deceiving men.
We have no regard for distinctions of caste in our adornment, nor do we indulge in excessive passion;
we have no attachment to the lips during union with a particular man. (DKuṭṭ 310)

Those who are full of passion even for a child, who harbor the onset of amorous desire even for the elderly, who look with longing at a eunuch as if he were a lover, and who feel desire even for one afflicted by a chronic disease— [such women are truly wretched].
Though covered with droplets of perspiration, their minds dwell upon their own lack of moisture;
though manifesting trembling, they are as hard as the core of a diamond-stone.
The courtesans are fickle-hipped, ignoble, like cuckoos, and possess feigned passion in their eyes;
they are skilled at offering all their limbs, yet withhold the region of their hearts.
Though born of the *nakula* lineage, they are well-acquainted with the pain caused by the bite of a serpent;
though they are illuminators of passion (*kandarpadīpikā*), they are devoid of any inclination toward affection.
Even when abandoned by their husbands during the time of dalliance, they are indifferent to any particular man;
though devoted solely to Kṛṣṇa, they are constantly fond of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Like mountains with their ridges frequented by thousands of *kiṃpuruṣas*,
and like the policies of kings whose association with calamities is well-avoided.
Like lotus ponds, they attain prosperity by drawing in many friends and kings;
and like ḍākinīs, they possess skill in attracting those who are impassioned.

Like the *prakṛtis* (primordial elements), courtesans are difficult to grasp; they are present with every man, intent on their tasks, equipped with various wiles, and like the elements, they seize many objects of interest.
Having embraced for a long time with respect both a cluster of flowers and a distinguished man,
the base and the lowly alike kiss them in order to empty them of their contents.
Even though they are extremely hard by ultimate nature, magnets and prostitutes attract iron and men who have fallen under the sway of sense objects. (DKuṭṭ 320)
Constantly trodden upon by men, made charming by artificial passion and amorous gestures,
with their hips being struck— both female elephants and courtesans are alike.
Even when raised by their accustomed virtues, beautiful women and scales exceeding in skill fall instantly with their faces [or pans] downward as soon as a fragment of gold is placed before them.
Having their beauty produced only on the outside, while being hollow within and hard by nature,
these female slaves creak like small boxes when operated by a mechanical device.
Those who, struck by fate, bind their affection to those courtesans,
will surely depart with their two hands placed before them [in supplication].
While her friend was thus instructing her and Sundarasena was tormented by love,
three songs were sung by someone who had approached us.

The dull-witted man who, having brought a young woman of lovely form under his control by means of the god of love, avoids her without falling into delusion— he is the first true "reed" (nālīka), provided he is not mistaken for a lotus stalk.
For this alone is the fruit of birth, this alone is the fruit of life for men:
that their youth passes away in the pleasure of union with lovely-hipped women.
Women whose every limb is being consumed by the rows of flames from the fire of the flower-arrowed god of love,
and who are devoted to intense passion, do not desire those of meager merit.
Having heard these words, the son of Purandara said to his friend:
"This has been sung by this virtuous man as if he had drawn it from my very heart."

"O Guṇapālita, let us go to comfort her who is bereft of the arrows of the bodiless god (Kāma), whose necklace is disarrayed, and whose eyes are as tremulous as those of a young fawn; what is the use of many deliberations?"
Then, at a certain place, a courtesan who was counting her familiar clients from whom she had taken wealth blocked a man as he was entering the house under the pretext of jealousy.
A certain courtesan, seeing the tattered old garment given by a swindler,
despaired at the end of the night when she had to attend to her livelihood.
A single female servant, seeing him fallen within her range of vision by the power of fate, her pride shattered,
rushed forward with speed and seized him, blazing with rage.
Another procuress spoke to a man who had lost his wealth and was standing at the door of the house of a wanton woman living within: "Go, you whose body is like a wave! (DKuṭṭ_334)
Another courtesan, displaying the wounds from teeth and nails inflicted during her amorous combat with the prince,
displayed her good fortune before her friends as she recounted the story.
Another courtesan, her fee increased by the rivalry of other lovers, raised high her *kheḍā* gesture and bore the pride of the vanity of her good fortune amidst the assembly of gallants.
A certain procuress, rushing forward in agitation, prevented a quarrel between a courtesan’s suitor, who was brandishing a weapon in a fit of rage, and her rival.
"Having gathered wealth from many, it is enjoyed by one together with someone"—
thus did a certain courtesan entice a wealthy man who was full of desire.
Then a certain lecher, singing even a mere two-line verse with great skill,
wandered through the city, performing all manner of contortions before a maidservant.
A certain lover, having fallen into poverty, used to provide for his courtesans by arranging their union with wealthy men out of passion.
"Because I was attached to you, I abandoned my home; now you have become like a stranger.
Thus did a certain man reproach a courtesan, failing to obtain her favor.
Having defeated another man who had been staying with her before a group of elderly libertines,
a certain rake forced the courtesan to pay double the fee.
"O Viśeṣaka, did you see Śaśiprabhā with her bracelets and armlets?
Tell me, tell me truly—how much more beautiful is she than the one given by me? (DKuṭṭ 343)
Today is the fourth day since the pair of fine garments was given;
yet my amorous charms remain harsh. Tell me, Madanaka, what shall I do in this matter?
"O Kelīkalahaṃsaka, she is indeed devoted to me; however, her mother is a Rākṣasī, and that wicked woman cannot be won over even in a hundred years."
"Prepare the jasmine and saffron perfumes; why do you stand there distracted?
Today, O Kiñjalkaka, is the occasion for the dance of your beloved."
O Kandarpaka, even if Taraṅgavatī were to show you affection for five days merely upon seeing a fragment of wealth, what is the use of your vain pride?
"O fool, Lāsaka, who hates living beings, keep Harisena far away!
He is possessed by her, his son is occupied with her, and he is most dangerous."
O Moonrise, behold the majesty of the multitude of lovers as they wander with necks held stiffly above, having been granted a moment by the Kesara flower to drape its silken garment over them.
"O lover, you indeed wish to arrange the marriage of Madanasenā;
however, I desire that her mother’s face be turned away. (DKuṭṭ 350)
What kind of fruit is this for the ascetic’s penance— that he should drink wine with his own hand,
offered by Devadattā, who is reeling from intoxication, as the remnants of what she herself had drunk?
"Why has Līlodaya, the abode of the Kuvalayamālā, been abandoned now?
O brother, what can we do for him without the price of a slave girl?"
The night passes for Indīvaraka, whose entire wealth has been stolen,
as he now rubs the feet of Tilakamañjarī, O Mañjīraka.
Even now Madanikā does not entirely abandon her childhood nature;
nevertheless, O Makarandaka, by her maturity she holds all other women in contempt.
Having gone to Kubjā, you shall say to that merciless-hearted dance master:
"Why have you today caused this necklace and this delicate body to suffer such exhaustion?"
"Desist from this obsession with teaching the parrot chick, O Queen Suratā!
Your beloved husband is waiting outside, seated and looking for you. (DKuṭṭ 356)
"Exhausted from playing the lute, they have fallen upon the couch in the bedchamber;
raise up that Smaralīlā quickly, for the son of the Bhaṭṭa has arrived! (DKuṭṭ 357)
"O Mādhavī, what is this state of yours that remains as it is, even though I speak to you repeatedly?
You do not put on the ornament given by the son of Śrī Vigraharāja."
"O Mother Indulekhā, what can we do with such a vacant mind?
Though the golden palm tree has fallen due to her preoccupation with playing in the drinking water, she does not even perceive it."
"Out of anger, this ill-behaved woman did not let Nakula drink milk; thus, Kāmasenā does not eat, even though she is entreated again and again."
Protected by the son of Śrībala, the long-lived one—what need has he to conquer her?
Mukula, who abandons the state of happiness and remains day and night intent on rearing rams! DKuṭṭ_361 //
O Sulalita, your palm has become coppery red and swollen;
do not continue to play with the ball in this manner for much longer!
"O charming Domba Bhāti, this woman is first taken as a wife;
but once affection has arisen, you have power even over the life of Kusumadevī."
"Hand over the pledge now, if you have curiosity regarding Candrasenā;
once your business is concluded, you may give her whatever she desires."
O Mother, this son of Nagararoṭabhaṭṭa is not a supreme donor;
he is shameless and of deceitful conduct, even though he has been restrained again and again.
The sun always forcibly strips away all the garments of the army of amorous play; it does not give back even a single thread of wool, but instead devours the very cotton.
"Sister, that deceitful prince does not leave my house even for a moment;
he has blocked all opportunity for other men, like a sacred bathing place presided over by a naked mendicant."
Hearing such words uttered by lecherous men and procuresses,
and observing that brothel establishment, he entered the house of Dayitikā.
As he approached her side, Hāralatā honored him as if she were drawn toward him by longing, and as if bathed by the radiance of her affectionate eyes.
Having been introduced by her friend, who stood nearby in the proper manner with her head bowed,
Sundarasena spoke these words very humbly at that auspicious moment.
"O Priyadarśana, what is the use of these many compositions of piteous words from one afflicted by love?
Here sits Hāralatā; her life is dependent upon you."
May your youth pass, clear with effortless play, delightful through the continuity of spontaneous love,
and well-freed from the obstacles of other duties.
May your amorous dalliance be merciless, characterized by incessant longing, devoid of shame, lacking restraint in conduct, and constantly increasing in passion. (DKuṭṭ 373)
Thus, after the attendants had departed with their blessings,
the flower-armed god of love increased all the more within her limbs, which were now filled with the essence of confidential intimacy.
That which is worthy of unrestrained passion and appropriate to fresh love;
that which is delightful in youth and that which is the fruit of living.
Lack of discipline is indeed their ornament; vulgar conduct is indeed their great respect; fearlessness is indeed their elegance; and instability is indeed their source of dignity.
Seizing the hair is a favor; striking is a service; a bite is for joy;
scratching with the nails is a blessing; and the firm crushing of the body is an exaltation.
In which [act], kissing is eager for swallowing, pressing against the limbs longs for crushing,
and intense embracing desires entry within.
That which was fashioned as if by the bodiless Cupid, brought to brilliance as if by passions,
made steadfast as if by loves, and brought to full bloom as if by sentiments of erotic love.
Lack of boldness is a calamity, steadfastness is a failure to act, and discernment is a detriment;
that in which shamefulness is a lack of merit—such is the sexual union commenced by those two.
When the god of love blazes forth with a roar at the very outset,
the particular states of him who has grown so great are impossible to describe.
In the multitude of various techniques determined by the science of love for the two youths, who were rendered dull by innate passion, their proficiency became stained.

In that tumultuous onset of their unrestrained amorous play, there was nothing for those two that was not subject to their will, nothing that could not be expressed, nothing that required deliberation, nothing that needed concealment, and nothing that was unbearable.
The natural onset of passion rendered that sequence of various amorous flatteries, which the slender woman had practiced so well during the act of love, broken and scattered.

Who is capable of enumerating the movements of a lover and his beloved, who are immersed in the circle of passion and whose actions are taught by the preceptor of Love, illuminated by the true nature of desire?
The young woman, her body like a tender creeper, was not merely unshaken when her form was overcome by the firm man;
she attained joy, for indeed, the power of the mind-born [passion] prevails.
We do not know whether the lover entered the beloved, or the beloved entered the lover;
at that moment, their awareness of their own limbs completely vanished.
At the conclusion of their lovemaking, as her eyes were closed and her body motionless,
the shadow of the bodiless god (Anaṅga) became the sign for inferring the existence of her life-force.
With drops of perspiration gathered upon her and feeling embarrassed by the memory of their circular movements,
she shone all the more at the conclusion of their dalliance, her hair and ornaments disarrayed.
As the two of them, having offered their bodies without guile, regarded the entire world as consisting solely of bliss,
the night came to an end while their longing remained undiminished.
Exhausted by the crushing of her passion, yawning, moving slowly with faltering steps,
and her eyes clouded with sleep, Hāralatā emerged from the chamber of Vāsava.
Having prepared my side for him, I shared food and drink with him;
the night was passed in conversation, yet whatever was intended as an act of seduction remained unfulfilled.
An unrefined, weary, and dull-witted young Brahmin, for whom women are hard to find,
has departed from me in the night under the guise of a lover— like an untimely death.
I have no desire for abstinence even for a moment, nor do I have the power to strive for pleasures devoid of substance;
today I am merely tormented by this old man.
Because of the influence of liquor, while my lover was as if dead and I was submerged in the depths of his bed,
the night passed for me happily with sleep unbroken.
O friend, my lover of enchanting form— tender in his touch, sweet in speech, and full of playful jests— has come to me by the power of destiny.
Reclining on his couch, turned away, letting out slow sighs,
he was rendered utterly motionless by my command and drenched with perspiration.
"Friend, today this man stands with his passion cast away, sleep departed, longing for the end of the night; having stayed in the village, he is now abandoned and devoid of any further action."
Listen, friend, to one curious thing done today by a rustic lover:
with her eyes closed in the bliss of sexual union, I was released by him in fear, thinking, "She is dead."
Because we did not understand his character or his native land, and because he was deceitful and cunning,
we experienced from this prince the distress of being mocked like a mere vessel.
"Dear friend, I was taken away by force by the lord of the city in the presence of everyone;
how, then, can there be any injustice in this request for double the amount from one who has provided a pledge?"
"O woman of Kerala, from the way you walk with your hips swaying as if they were torn to pieces nail by nail,
I think you must have been enjoyed by a man from the South."
A drop on your lower lip, a string of jewels around your neck, and a hare-leap mark upon your pair of breasts—
these indicate that your lover is an expert in the science of the flower-weaponed god [Kāma], O Ketakī!
Thus listening at dawn to the voices of courtesans who had ceased their nighttime efforts,
he too went out to perform his duties as they were being carried out.
As his mind was captivated by her through the well-prepared offerings of passion, a year and a half passed while he experienced the pleasures of youth together with her.
Once, while wandering upon the terrace of a garden pavilion, engaging in confidential conversation with his hand held in the grasp of his companion’s hand,
Sundarasena—
The covering of the vast sky was spread out by a continuous succession of thick, dense threads;
it consisted primarily of tattered rags, cloth-patches, and old gourds, held together at their edges by sticks.
He saw a messenger approaching from afar with a hurried gait, his body soiled and his feet cracked and smeared with mud, while his garments were torn and his feet were covered in dust.
Gradually perceiving that he had drawn near, the son of Puraṃdara, with a meaningful mind, said: "Friend, here has arrived Hanumān."
Sundara, having quickly picked up the letter placed on the ground by him who had bowed with his head touching the surface of the earth, read it.
"Hail! From the illustrious city of Kusumapura, Purandara addresses Sundara, his words and syllables indistinct as he is overwhelmed by an inner surge of grief. (DKuṭṭ 411)

As you fell upon the path frequented by the deceitful, you did not count your stainless lineage, you disregarded what is proper for the twice-born, and you paid no heed to the reproach of others. (DKuṭṭ 412)
Born in a lineage whose ways are straight, whose conduct is free from the fault of double-tonguedness,
and who delight in the destruction of no other— how is it that you have become a serpent?

Where is your mouth, filled with the chanting of Vedic verses purified by sacrificial cakes; and where is the tasting of the flavors from the mouths of courtesans, scented with wine and spirits? (DKuṭṭ 414)

Where is the sudden, startling pang of pain born from tearing the *kuśa* grass, and where is the merciless scratching of nails during the union with a maidservant’s lover for the sake of pleasure? *DKuṭṭ_415*
Where is the state of having a face washed by tears from eyes agitated by the smoke of the three sacrificial fires,
and where is this flood of tear-water brought on by the weight of grief from being insulted by a courtesan?
Where is the sound of the *vaṣaṭ* call, an ornament for the six rites that fills the ears, and where is the longing to hear the amorous cooing of common women? (DKuṭṭ 417)
On one hand, there is the trembling born from the agitation of being struck by the slender vine-like limbs of the teacher;
on the other, there is the endurance of the harsh kicks of the feet of an angry courtesan.
Where is the vow prescribed by the Smṛti scriptures for one who wears a deer-skin as a covering, and where is this great regard for wearing garments touched by the bodies of courtesans? (DKuṭṭ 419)
Having practiced the cutting of sacrificial fuel-sticks since childhood, from where has this skill of yours for biting the lips of deceitful women arisen? (DKuṭṭ 420)
Service to the guru alone was constantly practiced by you with an unwavering mind;
how then were those of crooked intellect, the slaves, skillfully propitiated by you?
The excellence of your words, so clearly refined by the recitation of the sacred scriptures, is well known;
but where did you learn such skill in speech as this for appeasing an enraged courtesan?
Or rather, what can be done? Even those born into this pure family become unacquainted with the assembly due to the fault of previously accumulated karma.
"Having entrusted my family to you, I shall remain with my soul solely intent on acquiring merit for the sake of the next world"—this desire of mine has been daily frustrated. (DKuṭṭ 424)

When Sundarasena was thus bewildered by the meaning of the letter he had read, another man sang an Āryā verse, accompanied by a song, at that opportune moment: DKuṭṭ_425: "When the meaning of the written message has been determined and Sundarasena is rendered helpless with confusion, another man sang an Āryā verse, adorned with a melody, on this very occasion."
For those men whose eyes are shrouded by the cataract of sense-objects and who fall into the pit with their path unseen,
the medicinal ointment of the staff-like words of their elders is their only refuge.

The application of bitter medicine and the harsh words spoken by a teacher cause distress at the time, yet they bring about the attainment of happiness in the end; so too does the task commanded by a guru. (DKuṭṭ 427)
Then, having found an opportunity for speech, he spoke to his friend, the son of Purandara:
"For the virtuous do not weary of speaking what is beneficial to those they hold dear."
For you, whose body is submerged in the great ocean of evil addiction and who disregard the words of your companions,
your father— agonized by grief— has nothing left to rely upon but his speech.
O Sundara, your father, who was the lamp of his own lineage, adorned by his virtuous deeds, and a being of great courage, has now been defiled by the fault of having a wicked son.
For a man of noble birth who possesses a son, the absence of a son is better than having a wicked one;
for the latter causes intense internal torment during conversations concerning the accounts of virtuous conduct.
In the world, those who are exalted by their virtues are generally restricted to the conventional realm alone;
yet that son for whose sake a mother boasts of her barrenness is the most wretched of men.
Knowledge of the scriptures is fruitless, and even service in the teacher’s house does not bring benefit to one whose mind is enslaved by sense objects and who abandons the path of righteousness.
Even while living, such a person is as good as dead, for when people see his face,
they contort their own features and point him out from afar with their fingers.
It is true that sense objects cannot be avoided; nevertheless, those of subtle intellect do not become the objects of expression when they are designated by a term qualified by its negation.
Service to the guru, a wife born of noble family, association with affectionate kinsmen,
and devotion to the sacred rites— these are the means for the wise to achieve success in both worlds.
Prosperity is easily attained by him, his virtues spread throughout the world, good people hold him in high esteem, and his kinsmen always long for him. (DKuṭṭ 437)
He alone does not encounter a stumble by following the path frequented by the virtuous;
he adorns his lineage, and that is the abode of all blessings without exception.
He becomes a repository of discipline, possessing the discernment between what is appropriate and inappropriate;
for him, the words of the instructions of the elders always serve as a nourishment for the ears.
The attachment of embodied beings to lowly women is the ripening of past karma;
yet noble-born women are the very abode of the pleasures found within the realm of saṃsāra.
When he is weary, she is weary; when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he is agitated, she is agitated.
Like a reflection, the beloved is joyful when he is joyful, but when he is enraged, she is merely afraid.

Only the wives of the meritorious are born with the capacity to endure the exertion of desired sexual union, who avoid discordant speech, and who are skilled in following the inclinations of their husbands' hearts. (DKuṭṭ 442)
Fearing the sound of her bracelets, she offered herself quietly, surrendering her limbs while manifesting the intent of the flower-arrowed god of love through the essence of her true affection.
"Alas, alas! O shameless one, why do you act so insolently and speak at will?
Have you completely forgotten that your attendants are standing nearby, even as you are tormented by love?"
Thus, with words and phrases that convey their meaning through grunts of assent,
the woman of noble family doubles the efforts of the hero during the expansion of his delusive power.
To his friend who had spoken thus, the son of Purandara,
trembling with the fear of imminent separation from life, replied with these words:
O father, while your command is not to be transgressed, and while the fierce fire of separation from Hāralatā burns within us,
