we do not know the ultimate outcome of our situation, for death now holds sway by the power of fate.

Drawn by fate, he abandons his beloved— who disregards the acquisition of wealth and whose mind is bound solely by affection— just as one might break apart a vessel forged with iron and diamond chips.
Then, having resolved to depart, he informed his beloved wife of the matter;
she too, her journey about to begin, followed him, overwhelmed with grief.
Having reached the foot of the banyan tree, her eyelashes moistened with drops of tears and the movement of her feet impeded, she spoke to Hāralatā:
"There is a saying that one should follow a loved one as they depart for a distance of a milk-bearing tree or a body of water; therefore, you must turn back from here."
"What can we do, O slender-waisted one? Struck by fate, that unimpeded arrow of the Teacher’s command—which violently severs the knot of love—is now prevailing."
There is no acquisition of heaps of wealth, no familiarity with a single patron, nor the quality of flattery; there is no command from a master, no seduction by outward appearance, and no fame.
Although you have no reason to act toward us, nevertheless, by the power of fate,
there exists such a connection that its ripening is beyond remedy.
O fair-toothed one, that which was spoken harshly by you out of jealous anger, or suspected jestingly—
do not remember it, for it is but the clamor of proclaiming ill-spoken words.
This heart has been placed within your heart; the preservation of this deposit is difficult.
You must therefore exert effort so that there may be no displacement from its place.

Then, having somehow restrained her speech— which was choked by a flood of tears and whose syllables were distressed by the weight of her emotion— Hāralatā spoke these words with a voice that had almost fainted away.

Born of an impure lineage, living by the offering of my body, and practicing deceit—where am I, a woman who lives by her beauty, and where are you, whose birth and virtues are praiseworthy? (DKuṭṭ 458)
"That which has rested here for so many days by one who came out of curiosity to behold the sights— that is the fruit of the merit I performed in a previous life."
Who, having developed an attachment through long-standing familiarity and observation, would abandon service to their guru, their kinsmen, their residence in their own country, and a favorable wife?
This fickleness of youth is that which causes you to feel curiosity toward someone like me;
however, the place where blameless happiness resides is one's own wife.
Those sweet jests, those crooked words, and that period of perverse behavior—
these must not be taken to heart by you when alone, if you desire your own welfare.
Whatever conduct I have performed that was contrary to you, whether out of negligence or through the influence of my mind, O Lord, I offer this salutation with joined palms upon my head.
The paths are difficult to traverse, the dwelling is far away, and the heart is unsteady;
therefore, O Guṇapālita, your friend must remain vigilant.

While the two youths, their hearts having attained oneness as they experienced the suffering born of separation, were engaged in conversation, another person recited this wholesome verse by chance: DKuṭṭ_465: "The heart is one for the two who are united; it is divided when there is separation."
For those bound by the firm bonds of affection and the reality of their mutual conduct,
death causes separation, or for the steadfast, it is the final severance.
Then, immediately after hearing that, Sundarasena said, "Stay here happily, my beloved; I am going," and as he departed slowly, he turned his neck back toward her.
With her arms hanging down from the branch of a banyan tree, her lips and mouth withered by the warm breath of her sighs, she lay prostrate,
her unblinking eyes fixed upon the path he had taken.
Her braid was swaying, her neck-ornament was askew,
her face was filled with flowing tears, and her vine-like limbs were exhausted as she lay fallen upon the edge of her garment.
As if it were crushing her heart with one hand while the other rested upon her pair of breasts—
she who had been abandoned by all her charms after they had fulfilled their duties toward the world of the living.
Hāralatā, who had accepted her misfortune and was brought under control by cruel strikes at her vital parts, was being drawn inward by Bhāratī, whose presence within her was not yet fully manifest.
"Do not go yet! Wait for a single moment until this pitiless man is hidden from view by the forest thickets!"—as she was speaking thus, her life-breaths departed.
Then, later on, the son of Purandara questioned a traveler who had arrived: "Have you seen a woman returning, distressed by grief? (DKuṭṭ 473)
He said: "A woman lies beneath the banyan tree on the ground with her limbs motionless; no other has come within the range of our vision."
Thus, struck by those words like a stone, his body reeling, he fell upon the surface of the earth;
and having been raised up by his friend, who was himself distressed with grief, he was addressed by him.
"Let my father have his purpose fulfilled, and you too, O Sumitra, rest now with a joyful heart;
for at the very same moment, Hāralatā has been released by me from both sin and life."
Alas, alas! O coquetry, you are slain; O playful charm, you are destroyed—what can you do?
O artful grace, you are cut off; O bewilderment, roam through the ten directions without support.
O *kilakiñcita*, go to the forest; O *moṭṭāyita*, you have met with helplessness;
O *kuṭṭamita*, take up the life of a wandering mendicant; O *bibboka*, enter a hole in the earth! (DKuṭ_478)
Once she has become the object of my longing, there is no destination for me to go;
when she, who steals the splendor of the moon’s orb, has departed, I shall go to the presence of Death.
I shall turn back and go to burn her who has abandoned her life in my absence;
let there be for that wretched woman the mere gift of the seven-flamed fire as a favor.
Then, having gone to that place where she had passed away into the five elements,
he rolled on the ground, uttering cries of lamentation, his body supported by his companion.
"We have desisted; abandon your anger, O wrathful one, and speak a word.
Arise! Why do you remain on the ground, your body covered in dust?"

O lady of beautiful countenance, why do you stand here with eyes closed in hesitation? It is not because of any offense on my part that I am forbidden from entering; there is no fault in me for following the rule of unobstructed access to you.
Now that you have departed for heaven, Madana is currently unarmed, even though his five arrows still remain, as he is unable to overcome the wives of the lords of the gods.
O beloved, that widespread reproach among people that courtesans live by deceitful means has been skillfully removed by you through the liberation of this living being.
Worthy of homage is Mahāsena, the sole son of the Destroyer of Tripura, who observes the noble vow;
his heart has not been touched even in the slightest degree by love for a woman with beautiful eyes.
I believe that, having determined separation from one's beloved to be unbearable even for the blink of an eye,
Hari held Lakṣmī upon his chest, while Hara held Gaurī as half of his own body.
O Guardian of the World, did you not consider that she was the ornament of the earth and that the entire universe would be empty without her, as you led your beloved away from her own place?
O Lord Fire, do not, having extracted the very essence of the ocean of beauty,
burn her up— she who has somehow been fashioned by the Creator as the ornament of the world.
Disregarding the son of Purandara as he lamented in many ways,
the friend constructed a funeral pyre with wood and committed the courtesan to the flames.
While his mind was agitated by grief, having resolved upon casting himself into that blazing fire, someone recited by chance an Āryā verse that flashed across his mind: *DKuṭṭ_491*
What person possessed of discernment would resolve upon following [her husband] in death as a duty of women,
except for one who has taken up the staff and the vow that is the means for liberation from saṃsāra?
Having heard this, Sundarasena, his despondency dispelled, said to his minister:
"My mind has been awakened by this wise man who has given such appropriate instruction."
In this revolving cycle of existence, which is overwhelmed by birth, old age, sickness, and death— where loved ones are seen and lost in an instant— what person of sound mind would harbor attachment?
May you go to Kusumapura; we too shall undertake residence in the final stage of life (antyāśrama), as prescribed for the complete accomplishment of the abandonment of ignorance.
That noble man said: "Since childhood you have never been separated from me;
how can you now abandon the resolve for renunciation toward a friend who is free from desire for sense-objects?"
Having said "So be it," Sundarasena, accompanied by Guṇapālita, went to the forest frequented by ascetics whose vows were firmly established.
"Let it be so; courtesans are focused solely on their own self-interest and devoid of true virtue. Yet, what loss is there for you in the accomplishment of your desired objects? (DKuṭṭ 498)
The discussion of ultimate reality does not touch the hearts of clever courtesans, who are skilled in the sixty-four arts and adept at following the desires of lovers.
Through the movements of bending, leaping, various gaits, and standing, and by following the rider's impulse, the horse of the riders enters [the path] even without the touch of passion. (DKuṭṭ 500)
From where could there be even a scent of love for the cuckoos, the *hārīta* birds, and the domestic pigeons?
Nevertheless, they stir the passion of young men with their particular calls that kindle the fire of the god of love.
An actor, though devoid of actual emotion, brings delight to the minds of the audience by means of the perfect accomplishment of his entire performance, which is applied with skill and effort.
Even those dull-witted men who perceive the fault of wasting wealth in the embrace of wanton women should be asked by you: "Are wives not themselves the expenditure of a lifeless funeral shroud?"
Furthermore, gain alone is not the sole cause for engaging in sexual activity among humans;
passion and other such factors also exist, as stated by the authors of the treatises on erotics.
What power was attained by that ascetic woman from Sundarasena,
she who, shattered by the thunderbolt of separation from him, gave up her life in half a moment?

Who can ward off the erotic sentiment, which possesses the nature of supreme youthfulness, whose attachment to another body is indicated by horripilation and the like, and whose manifest emotional state is clearly present?

Even in the presence of their elders and attendants, those skilled in the ways of unchaste women perceive the transformation of their inner hearts through a glance made sweet by the contraction of the brow and the corners of the eyes.
Abandoning their husbands' homes without a thought for family disgrace or public reproach, other women—
whose hearts are stained by passion— depart for distant lands, leaving men behind.
For those women whose virtue is destroyed by disrespect from their husbands, the severity of their elders' entourage, or even poverty at home,
there arises through passion an attachment to another man.
Even those women who are of unswerving conduct and devoted to the service of their husbands remain free from passion, abiding merely by virtue of propriety.
Therefore, let there be visiting [of women] for various reasons; who can prevent it?
However, the fulfillment of the heart’s desire regarding one's own or another's wife as a commodity depends entirely upon passion.
With such examples supported by reasoning, with words of this kind,
and with other flattering phrases as well, one should approach her whose mind has been won over.
At the departure of night, having embraced him firmly with a yawn that had been provoked, she revealed a slight exhaustion and languor from her sleep, though it was regulated by her own will.
Having surveyed the quarters with eyes whose lids were unsealed, and heaving a long sigh, she said:
"O Night, you must be told this: why have you departed to the wicked?"
How could a weak woman endure the flow of the essence of human pleasure possessed by one of firm power,
were it not for the passion born of desire providing her with strength?
Blessed is the wife of the Cakravāka bird by virtue of attaining the moment of union with her beloved;
O night-lily, being separated from the moon, you are one whose merit is exhausted.
A fresh flower, though its form is blossomed, fragrant, and enchanting,
does not cause such pain to a female bee when it has fallen after being tasted as it does when it has not yet been reached.
Therefore, having bowed with my head and hands joined in reverence, I make this request of you:
by your grace, may I be counted among your circle of attendants.

Then, having inspired confidence by means of soft, agreeable attentions— characterized by limbs glowing with passion, casting aside the sequence of gains and honors, and accumulated through long practice— he was brought low.
"You have been observed, you lecher! What are you whispering so secretly into the ear of Śaṅkarasena’s nursemaid? Today, I [have seen it] through the lattice window."
"There is no contradiction in your engaging in play with Mālatī, thinking, 'She is my friend';
however, as for the fact that you gaze upon her for so long with an affectionate look, there I have my suspicion."
"I have come to see you, yet I was neither detained nor entreated with effort.
Tell me, having summoned her, for what purpose was Kamaladevī made to take betel?"
Did you not notice with intense focus Kundamālā as she was pulling off her bodice, revealing her shoulders, armpits, breasts,
and sides?
If you caught hold of me by the hem of my garment in jest,
why did you suddenly snatch it away and flee when you saw me from behind?
While Kusumalatā is renowned for her discernment, you instead describe her incessantly as Mṛgadevī dancing, gazing at her with wide-open eyes.
I do not know the reason for this, that you always abandon the well-known straight path and travel by a winding route along the front of Mādhavasenā’s house.

Thus, O slender-waisted one, when her deep-rooted passion was made known through these and other jealous remarks— words arising from affection that were light-hearted yet piercing to the vital spots— iti serṣyopanyāsairanyaiścāmarmavedhilaghukopaiḥ / praṇayaprabhavairvidite cchātodari rūḍharāgatve // DKuṭṭ_527 //
O long-eyed one, with your body hidden from the range of hearing, you have established your presence here with your mother;
why then would you engage in such a quarrel of false words with harsh speech?
One whose wealth was acquired without effort, who was humble with affection, and whose generosity was unrestrained—
this son of Bhaṭṭānanda, who was like a treasure, has been abandoned by you, an ill-fated woman.
"O foolish woman, his discernment destroyed by calamity and his sole refuge being fate, this Lord Keśava— who hates his own wife— has been insulted by you, disregarding me."
Disregarding the danger of the king and naturally inclined toward unceasing generosity,
why was the superintendent of customs ignored or even befriended by one of such perverse intellect?
The father had only one son; when he reached his fourth decade and was overcome by disease, the wealthy man, desiring misfortune for him, cast that son out, though he was his rightful heir.
"O sinful woman, what can I do? You have abandoned your own prosperity by your own hand, while looking with disdain upon Vasudeva who has come to you with his entire burden."
"You have not even asked about that man who, his mental state incited by rivalry with others, impulsively bestows wealth without regard for anything else."
Skilled in the arts such as painting and proficient in the science of love, though he was of a virtuous nature and helpful to all, you have cast him among the ranks of your enemies.
"O passionate woman, do you not feel shame, seeing and wearing this ornament of Candravatī given by the son of Madhusūdana?"

While browsing among the thorny, bitter-tasting shrubs, trees, and thickets such as the *karīra* and *khadira*,
a female camel by chance encounters a sweet cluster of honey.

What is prosperity for one who is not under the sway of a lover? What is the playfulness of those devoid of the god of love? What dharma is without tranquility? And what is the happiness of those separated from their beloved?
Childhood has freedom as its fruit; youth has the enjoyment of desired sexual pleasure as its fruit;
old age has tranquility as its fruit; and the fulfillment of the welfare of others is the fruit of birth.
Having overheard this from her friend as she spoke it, [the maiden] said: "As if seized by a spirit, you have been separated from me along with the pleasures of youth."
Now, standing in the midst of the fire of remorse, with all my limbs being cooked,
I live on by a mere breath, having attained a birth that is utterly fruitless.
In those places where I have long played with you in joyful companionship,
as I gaze upon them now, my life-breath indeed stands at the very throat.
Under the power of another, rendered unconscious and adorned with ornaments, moved by the mechanism of strings—
like a wooden statue, I perform many such farces.
If she clings to other flowers merely to fill her belly,
even that does not bring nourishment to the female bee who does not drink the nectar of the lotus.
Let alone other worlds; let alone one who delights in the misfortunes of others for sport—I was not prevented by my attendants as I was falling into this ocean of calamity.
What is the use of much speaking? My mind is now restrained by this vow; thus disciplined, I shall remain in your house to perform the tasks of a servant.
Thus, brought under control by the distortions of his eyes and other features, his bodily firmness dissolved,
overcome by the demon of Māra, he lost all memory of his former appearance.
O fair-browed one, as soon as he manifests a desire for dalliance and casts his gaze toward the region of your throat moment by moment,
you shall drink him dry, leaving nothing behind, just as one sucks a ripe mango, as before.
Having cast out the hook of crooked smiles, glances, and speech smeared with the bait of one's own body,
he draws in the dull-witted man— devoid of movement yet thoroughly fattened.
Having prepared it with the expenditure of ritual offerings,
once you have eaten it, you will leave behind only the skin and bones of the fish, having cast away all its flesh.
Listen, O fair-hipped one, how in this very place at the feet of Kalaśeśvara, by Mañjarī,
the daughter of the preeminent teacher, the prince was both chewed and released.
There was a king named Śrī Siṃhabhaṭa, the foremost among the most illustrious;
his son occupied the residence connected to Devarāṣṭra.
Once, desiring to see the one whose banner is the bull, he went forth accompanied by a limited circle of trusted attendants,
following the youthful fashions of dress and conduct.
He had his hair bound up with a large cloth strip positioned at the upper third of his head;
his body was lightly tinted with red pigment, and the tips of his ears and hair were smeared with thick saffron.
Having used betel-leaf with the seeds of the *siddhārtha* plant as tooth-cleansers and a tilaka mark upon his forehead,
he wore earrings set in his ears and a necklace consisting mostly of *ṭīṭibhaka* birds around his neck.
He wore a resinous pill containing mantras, encased in gold and positioned where an armlet would normally sit;
and upon his wrists he had placed a string of precious gems with dangling sprouts of gold.
Holding a staff of cane, with a small sword sheathed in a woolen scabbard at his waist, covered by a very soft cloth, and wearing sandals that made a loud *curcur* sound as he moved; DKuṭṭ_742 //
"Your heroic friend, it is said, has fallen in love with the maidservant of Gambhīreśvara;
even she shall obtain in three years of ill-gotten hope that which was obtained by me."
"Suradevī, Candravarman points out the directions as if they were bearing fruit and lowers his hand as if it were a ray of nectar, through a proliferation of words devoid of substance. (DKuṭṭ 744)
"O Kuraṅgī, I see Vasuṣeṇa following right after you now;
you will find out for yourself how deceptive his 'sweet-tongued' nature truly is."
O Hariṇī, that Hara who, out of pride in his cunning,
chews water and writes down a hundred with an increase of ten— he is now submerged in the whirlpool of Taralikā.

"Since you, O Nanda, are taking the woman named Madirā from the hem of my garment while I am looking on, you will certainly not fail to speak of it; for there can be no difference between what has been said and what has not been said."
This Kuśakarṇa, who has taken up his grass mat, holds his staff and saffron robe;
fearing contact with the world, he has withdrawn and is looking toward both sides.
Observing a vow of silence and having inspired faith in all the Vaiṣṇavas,
he took refuge in the command of Hari under the pretext of visiting the Destroyer of Tripura.
She gazes at me with longing through a clever artifice, her glance avoiding the sight of others; O Night-lily, this must surely be a pretext for my heart's desire.
He sees while remaining unseen; when scrutinized, he gazes toward the far horizon.
He says something with longing, yet when addressed, his speech becomes stilled.
"He does not leave his vicinity, nor can he bear to remain within the range of touch;
I think this man is both speechless and full of longing."
Gone indeed are those days when we shared jests with you;
now you are a teacher’s wife by virtue of your connection to a teacher of pure conduct.
"O Lolikadāsa, you may wander at will, plucking the sprouts of young women,
for as long as you do not enter the noose of Naradevī."
The temple was crowded with lecherous servants and maids engaged in such talk, while its path was cleared by attendants skilled in service.
Having performed his worship of Śiva, Samarabhaṭa took his seat upon a throne placed there by swift messengers, while the world was brought under control by the harsh Niṣṭhurāṣṭaka.
In front sat a group of young women accompanied by dancers, flute-players, and singers;
there were also betel, flowers, and aromatic powders presented by the merchants led by the guild-president.
It was not empty of those bearing swords with blades whetted on various whetstones and held in their hands,
nor of head-guards and guardsmen who carried daggers at their backs and were full of confidence.
Holding the betel-box,
with his left hand— its fingers in the *khaṭakāmukha* position— he gently touches the end of the betel-roll held by the pincers.
Having shifted the weight of his body onto the front part of his frame, which was supported by his dear and humorous ministers standing at his side,
he inquired after the welfare of the merchants, dancers, and others.
Then, as the clamor of the people was hushed by the bard, the steadfast man praised him in this way with a voice that was clear and profound:
Victory to you, O God, destroyer of the enemy forces, whose mind is solely intent on worshipping the feet of the Guru;
who uses the hips of another's wife as his seat, and who possesses a fierce mass of rays like the sun to dispel the darkness of poverty.

O ornament of the lineage of heroes in battle, you who are humble in worshiping the Guru, the Earth, and the Gods; O bestower of fearlessness upon those who seek refuge, you who are like the midday sun to the bandhujīva flower of your devoted kinsmen.
Such is your fire of majesty, which pervades the circle of the sky and all directions;
it is seen acting like water upon the beauty of the forehead-ornaments of the wives of your enemies.
This is the clear distinction between ordinary fire and the fire of your majesty:
that which is burnt by the former sprouts again, but for that which is burnt by this, there is no further rebirth.

Your host of adversaries, though their fortune has been snatched away, does not relinquish its hold on the kingdom; they subsist on wood-apples, clothe themselves in leaves, take pleasure in physical exertion, and have abandoned their delight in sacrificial feasts.
Having abandoned your house— you who always gave desired wealth and were ever devoted—
your fame, through the fickleness of women, has gone naked in all directions.
Your fortitude is such that even Andhaka was shattered by it and bowed down;
yet you have liberated many enemies who were merely onlookers in battle.
While wandering over the entire world, I have seen this marvel:
that even you, O delighter of the eyes, avoid contact with the fierce.
This is another most wonderful thing: that while being plundered by thousands of young women, the treasury of your good fortune increases rather than diminishes.
Furthermore, that whiteness of yours, which produces wonder,
does not fade even when variegated by the luster of the blue-lotus petals of women's eyes.
O Puruṣottama, wielder of the flower-weapon, you dwell as one within the hearts of many women; it is for that reason, O Janaka, that you possess a universal form.
O Lord of Men, why do you vainly harbor the pride that "I am beloved by women"?
Sixteen thousand gopīs once longed for Murāri.
Hṛṣīkeśa, who at the time of the sacrifice entreated Bali for his brahminical status,
is not equal to you, whose heart is solely intent upon giving.
Standing above all who bear the earth by your loftiness, when will you not be as skillful as a cloud in removing the torment of thirst for the entire world of living beings?
Though possessing many paths, full of devious turns, intent on crooked ways, and skilled at causing divisions among lineages,
the flow of the Ganges' waters is equal to yours only in its direction toward merit.
The origin of wicked conduct, the birth of folly, and the dwelling place of lack of discernment—
you alone are the knower of faults, by whom the Kali age has been made successful.
Even the Sugata does not turn away from his life’s mission, nor is the bull-bannered Śiva possessed of despondency;
yet you, though with sword raised against the enemy, have become one whose blade hangs down—why is this?

O King, it is truly marvelous that you are embraced by all virtues—[you who are] like a genuine jewel, possessing manifold enjoyments, capable of bearing heavy burdens, and a stable abode for the self. (DKuṭṭ 779)
How can he be equal to Piṅgala, by whom the naturally light and low-caste Jaghanacapalā was made to attain dignity, just as the Āryā [was made to attain it]? 780.
O Bhavasāra, you are not equal to that proponent of non-duality for whom there is no birth, no self, no cognition of objects, and no mental tranquility.
Even there, there is an increase in prosperity; even in that, there is renown for a multitude of human virtues.
Even in that regard, you do not exceed grammar through its technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*). (DKuṭṭ 782)
O Lord, though you are beyond praise, free from all censure, and incomparable, you adorn the earth with the qualities of your true form, nature, and virtues.
This description of yours is indeed unique; you stand before us as something truly transcendent. Just as you are adverse toward enemies, you are equally adverse toward friends.
O Prince, because you honor your elders, because you delight in the conduct of the virtuous,
and because you satisfy the brahmins, for that reason you are a *vṛṣala*.
This is a wretched thing that you boast even of being equal to a Rākṣasa;
he did not act with violence toward his wife, yet you forcibly enjoy the fortune of your enemy.
That hymn of charming and flattering words which is the cause of our gain falls upon your own true nature; I offer my salutations, may there be happiness.
Immediately upon hearing this, he greeted the bard with words of praise and said: "Stay!
Why are you so agitated? You shall go away satisfied, sent forth by me."
Read once more that pair of songs which you previously recited while I stood hidden behind a curtain in the dwelling of the noble maiden.
While you were uttering words of praise, this speech was released within the assembly of the wise;
having thus spoken, he recited with a voice purified in its three places.
One is angry because of a quarrel, another is tasteless due to the embarrassment of a broken love-affair;
yet another, failing to reach a seat closer to him, harbors a deep despondency in her heart.
One woman has been separated by a quarrel, another is distressed by the shame of her recent marriage;
standing in the midst of a group of women, what can a man with many wives do when he is afflicted by love?
Making a nod of his head to signify his agreement, he, with knitted brows, said to the dance master:
"In this, what is well-sung? (DKuṭṭ_793)
Then he said: "Wherever the leaders of merchants carry their vessels, there are the abodes of deceit; how then can there be excellence in the dance of those slave-girls?"
One woman was stepped upon by a strong man; another did not leave her lover, however charming he might be; yet another spent the day in a drinking circle together with her friends.
One woman never leaves the door of the house, hoping for the arrival of a man;
meanwhile, the guard at the stake, having received a bribe, speaks of another woman who is in her menses.
Even while on stage, if a lowly woman hears that someone familiar has arrived at her house, she abandons her current role and goes there for the sake of a water-errand. (DKuṭṭ 797)
How can that woman, whose gaze was practiced upon her beloved from the first emergence of youth,
ever find favor with others when she stands in the midst of the assembly?

Mastery over the mind brings strength to a being, and when that strength exists, there is beauty in one's application; yet such mastery does not belong to courtesans whose hearts are set upon wine, meat, and men.
When Anaṅgaharṣa had gone to the world of the gods, the abode of the deities, we too, having no other recourse, took refuge here, despite the obstruction of this sacred site.
But here, at times, out of fear that something might obstruct their movements, they become dispirited;
in this *Ratnāvalī*, they perform these gestures of moving their hands and feet.
This [act] of hers, who is in the role of the Queen of Vatsa, imitates the companion of the King;
she mimics the performance of the character of Vāsavadattā.
Through the excellence of her effort and literary skill, and through her connection with me,
she has attained fame for this work composed by the daughter of the King of Siṃhala.
The arrangement of various postures, the graceful movement and flexion of the limbs,
speech whose meaning is articulated through modulations of tone, the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and the stability of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
The unfolding of sattvic states, acting, movement suited to the occasion, and ornamentation;
[the performers] describe the loss of tempo in both mixed and unmixed instrumental music in the *Mañjarī*. (DKuṭṭ 805)
This [woman], whose consciousness of the embodied Flower-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva) was destroyed by the mere mention of his name,
suddenly perceived the state of the Mind-born One through the opening of a *sinduvāra* flower.
Perceiving the Lord of Vatsa as indistinguishable from the character he portrays— due to the complete disappearance of the distinction between the actor and the role—
he brings joy to the minds of the audience, whose faces are made resonant with the sounds of his excellent performance.
While drawing the image of the Lord of the Vatsas, she gradually succumbs to the states of passion;
with trembling, horripilation, and perspiration, she causes her hand to become unsteady.

Even though the collection of attendant emotions (anubhāva-gaṇa) is similar, [the poet] demonstrates that the sentiment of compassion (karuṇa-rasa) is distinct from the sentiment of separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra),
as seen in the case of one who has fallen into the state of hanging herself without any further desire.
While he was thus pointing out Mañjarikā, the prince, looking at her with longing,
touched her with his cane, wondering, "Is this she?"
Then, perceiving his disposition, the minister spread a playful conversation about young women,
disparaging courtesans while praising the pursuit of prostitutes.
The pleasure with one's own wife is for the sake of progeny, and the embrace of a maidservant is for the alleviation of disease;
indeed, that alone is true sexual delight which is obtained with difficulty through other women.
My mind was never once intent on the affairs of others, being solely devoted to my own duties;
yet today, as I behold you in such a state, my heart is deeply pained.
If I know his dwelling place, and if I possess the power to do so,
then having gone there, I shall crush that cursed Fate with clubs.
O slender-limbed one, if such an incomparable form as this was fashioned for you by the Creator, why has he made its fruit barren by depriving it of a worthy lover? (DKuṭṭ 815)
Let there be childhood, old age, disease, or even hereditary consumption;
let there be youth in its natural form, but never one seized by the torments of a bad husband.
For an unfortunate householder, play burns the marrow, amorous passion consumes the bones, and harsh words sting; yet even giving does not bring satisfaction to his mind.
"From where have you come? At what time have you been standing here for so long? For what purpose?"—asking such things, the householder, with an uneasy mind, causes a headache. (DKuṭṭ 818)
If, by the turn of fate, a young man radiant with beauty comes within the range of his sight,
the master of the house squanders himself and his wife there, shouting [in joy].
In this world, which is full of disputes regarding the next life, public scandal, and manifold wonders,
and where destruction is subject to fate— the wise do not squander their youth.

O lady with beautiful breasts, your pair of high bosoms, though possessing great beauty, is defiled day by day by the striking of a wicked husband; thus, despite their loftiness, they are as good as fallen.
A couch with fine coverings, a compliant husband,
and a charming dwelling do not equal even a hundred-thousandth part of the pleasure of love-making practiced in secret for a fleeting moment.
That which is desired is obtained by one who has performed no small amount of virtuous karma, when suddenly encountering it on a path of peril, unexpectedly appearing before them.
Those who contemplate the world beyond have declared that heaven is indeed unsurpassed joy;
yet the attainment of that joy arises from union with a man desired by the heart.
Those dull-witted ones who resolve upon the effort to grasp sweet fruit that is not situated on its own branch become merely vessels for sorrow, affliction, and disease. (DKuṭṭ 825)
Is it an unfavorable planetary transit, or is it the ripening of misdeeds from another birth? Or is it the habitual practice of one's own actions by that destroyer whose origin is within himself?
By means of which that ascetic youth praises the wind touched by your limbs;
he longs for the region of the earth trodden by your feet and bows to the quarter of the sky inhabited by you.
He meditates upon your form and recites the rosary of syllables that are your name,
with a one-pointed mind, longing for the attainment of the bliss of union with you.
Having abandoned all other business, he gazes at you with his neck turned sideways,
making the street in front of his house swirl with hundreds of turns from his coming and going.
"You were seen by her for a long time wandering near the house with longing;
this is the message she has given, and this gift is sent to you."
"She withers away, seeking an opportunity to leave your house for your sake"—
thus is she being deceived by clever and deceitful women under the pretext of your name.
What is the use of further words to one whose mind is possessed by such an improper state?
Act as is appropriate; for from you depend both destruction and the protection of life.
A woman who approaches another man instantly accepts the ruin of her family, the reproach of the people, rebirth in hell, and the risk to her very life. (DKuṭṭ 833)
He writes a deed of slavery, abandons his family, and gives away all his possessions,
until the young woman of another appears before him with her garments cast aside.
"Whatever was to be seen has been seen; curiosity has passed away and is known within,"—having thus reflected in his mind, he then quickly performed what was required.
Severed and released from the grasp of the snapping [hand],
she entered the house trembling, looking toward all directions with apprehension and embarrassment.
When questioned out of agitation as to where she has gone— she who is not skilled in the various ways of a well-adorned unchaste woman due to the collapse of her new conduct— she replies, "Nowhere."
These faults are many, and men are generally fickle in their curiosity;
yet, being seized by you and bewildered by my duty, I remain here.
Thus, with her heart swinging like a swing, she was watched by the messenger who had steadied her through practiced artifice;
fearing she was being observed, she trembled at every step even at the rustle of a leaf.
Casting her eyes here and there, repeatedly startled and tremulous,
she arrived at the place of assignation, drawn by a hundredfold intensification of her desires.
Producing a mass of aesthetic sentiments blended with fear, passion, and modesty, she captivates through her shifting silken garments and the partial glimpses of her shoulders, breasts, and navel.
Preventing the beginning of the loosening of her girdle with repeated "No, no, I am not going,
I am going," she causes the duty of Love to sprout through her silent and indistinct words.
When another woman embraces him, she seems to swallow all his limbs and lead them to internal dissolution; yet for him, nectar itself would seem bitter in her presence.
In private, with your voice faltering as it was choked by tears, you did not utter those words that would have released the surge of grief caused by the insults from the master of the house.
Using our arms as pillows for one another,
we slept without hesitation, our thighs pressed together, our limbs relaxed, exhausted by the friction of lovemaking.
Having brought delicious food from my own home and concealed it in a secluded place, I gave it to you with my own hand; yet, with a heart full of contentment, you have ruined it.
I have not maintained my conduct, nor have I enjoyed your body as a well-ordered instrument;
fallen from both the seen and the unseen worlds, where shall I go, or what shall I do, I who am so ill-born?
Now, those who know my character laugh at me, a sinful woman, as I hide my face with my hands, delighting in the modesty of veiling myself, speaking only in private, and moving very slowly.
Those women of equal age and noble birth with whom I once shared friendship—now their guardians restrain me from them, saying, "This is bad company. (DKuṭṭ 849)
Enduring the insults of my attendants with a face bowed by suppressed anger,
I remain free from pride, owing to the weakness of the faults I have brought upon myself.
Hearing this praise of devoted wives being offered by the virtuous as a matter of incidental conversation, I, a fool, am sinking with a heart that is tormented.
Unable to restrain me as I sat down nearby due to my modesty,
my kinsmen, while eating, looked at one another and shrank back.
By not casting off the vicinity of our home for even a moment, and by not withdrawing your gaze— so deeply absorbed in us and so tender with love— you have made [your affection] manifest.
Those who portend the ruin of others' homes, who are arrogant due to their own perceived beauty and prideful of their charm,
and whose passion is like that of a chameleon— such are those like you.
Thus, with syllables choked by the grief arising from an undesirable way of life,
the fortunate ones hear the reproachful words of their courtesan in solitude.
For one whose gaze has been offered with affection toward the true essence of another's young wife,
the amorous charms displayed by a courtesan are said to be like withered grass before him.
A great festival of delight approaches for those who have propitiated specific deities;
even the words of a wanton woman, when moist with affection, reach the ears of the meritorious.
What need is there to mention that wretched man who delights in sense-objects and longs for another's wife?
Even the mere act of looking at her under a pretext touches the very marrow of those whose minds are fixed in meditation.
In heaven, courtesans bear his command with hands joined in reverence upon their heads;
yet even so, the Lord of Śacī, drawn by the passion for another's wife, consorted with Ahalyā.
Are the Apsarases not under the control of those possessed of wit, and is he not the foremost among the clever? For by what [reason] did Govinda form an attachment to the wives of cowherds?
The courtesans throughout the three worlds were under the command of the lord of the *yātudhānas*,
yet he even abducted the wife of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
Then Mañjarī’s mother, emboldened to support her own side,
began to refute the speech relied upon by the prince and his ministers.

One who was bold among the young women of the city, yet whose manhood was stolen by the sight of sophisticated courtesans, becomes a rustic, unrefined villager; such as you, O lady, will inevitably come to disparage a courtesan.

The amorous dalliance of an unfaithful wife with her living husband does not delight the minds of men who have studied the treatises of the God of Love, for it is devoid of nail-marks and tooth-wounds.
"Set down the water-jar for now; spread a covering of grass upon the ground.
Such is generally the beginning of lovemaking among rustic young couples."
An uncultivated libertine, his matted locks smeared with thick ushira-paste and adorned with a garland of kāṇa-mallikā flowers,
imagines himself to be the god of love when seen by a rustic woman.
Having emerged from her water duties, drenched in sweat from the exhaustion of household chores,
the low-born woman finds joy when her paramour approaches at the arrival of night.
When a woman has descended into a well with a water-jar and placed her feet upon a wooden beam,
her glance— casting her neck back to look up— elevates the heart of the young man.
On whichever limb you were touched by fate, however slightly, during her procession to the temple,
even today that limb does not release the bristling thrill of horripilation.
Having entered the empty, dense grove to gather cotton, she made a signal by clinking her sword; yet you, O fool, did not perceive it.
As she embraces the pestle with her eyes fixed solely upon you,
a hindrance has indeed arisen for the threshing of the rice, as she turns back and wanders before it.
She saw him throwing a bilva fruit, his prowess being praised by those standing nearby;
abandoning his household duties, she watched through the opening of the door.
O fortunate one, while you were standing near the road, she— unaware of her own distress—
compelled the people in the nearby houses to become victims of love-sickness.
Thus, the mind of the village libertine, filled with the pride of good fortune aroused and increased by the four female messengers, leaps up like a thousand waves.
Having restrained that expansion of speech with his head bowed low,
the dance master then spoke these words to the son of Śrī Siṃhabhaṭa.
On the stage of the hero, there are Bharata, the Kuśīlavas, and sages such as Kohala;
in the drama of women, there are the Apsarases and Gāndharva, the son of the Lotus-born One.
The sage Mataṅga is an expert in demonstrating the application of hollow-sounding instruments;
if they delight your heart, O dweller upon the earth, what power do you possess? (DKuṭṭ 877)
For those who live by their craft generally possess an excessive boldness,
especially for one who has lived as a dependent dancer and has conquered the stage.
Therefore, I inform you that you are like the Creator himself in this enacted drama;
please look upon this one scene so that my labor may not be in vain.
Speaking thus, urged by the son of the Lord of Men with a raised eyebrow,
he had the stage-manager appointed once all the musical instruments were prepared.
When the *sthānaka* (musical posture) given by Vāṃśika has been properly introduced with the *bhinnapañcama* melody,
the *sūtrī* enters during the interval of the two-footed verse (*dvipadī*) of the introductory *dhruvā*.
Endowed with a spirit of enthusiasm and delighting the hearts of the audience,
he [performs] through the totality of his own skill and mastery, as well as the poetic excellence of the deeds of the Lord of Vatsa.
Having circumambulated the *dhruvā* staff, which measures eight digits and is accompanied by rhythm and tempo,
he summons a dancer and engages in conversation with her regarding the affairs of his own household.
Having signaled the arrival of his attendants and taken a few graceful steps,
he departed together with his wife to the accompaniment of a song of departure.
Then, relying on the introduction of the story, the minister entered with wonder,
delighted by the king’s rise through such an improbable conjunction of events.
Pointing out the Lord of Vatsa— who was ascending the palace to witness the festive revelry of the Flower-Armed God (Kāma)— he departed in order to accomplish the task immediately following.
Then the lord of men, having ascended to his palace, entered together with his companion;
with a joyful heart, he gazed upon the delight [of the city] through the abundance of his own happiness.
Then, drawn by a state of wonder, with eyes wide open and shedding tears, he danced amidst the throng of citizens and cried out, "Friend, look! Look!"

The populace, their rasa of joy fully aroused, plays together—children, youths, and the elderly all alike; young women move about, some veiled and some unveiled; and they disregard what should or should not be said.
Tawny with the dust of fragrant powders, with an abundant array of various flowers artfully arranged,
and with songs and scattered words accompanied by many sighs arising from the fatigue of her limbs.
An old man, dancing with uplifted arms to the rhythmic clapping mixed with the sound of musical instruments,
repeatedly stumbling yet displaying firmness and grace.
"May springtime be eternal, with the embrace of a beloved woman who is entirely under one's control"—
singing thus, the young woman impetuously embraces [her lover] under the influence of intoxication.
Struck by the water from a horn while she was playing without any affection, the young man—
this wicked-souled one— considers himself fortunate because of the woman.
When the dam of modesty has been broken by the opportunity of a festive occasion, and a flood of vulgar speech flows forth from the face of a virtuous wife, who can restrain its spreading torrent?
For women whose speech is identical in its outward activity and who are intent on gambling,
the veil covering their faces serves to distinguish between the noble and the ignoble.
Then two maidservants entered, dancing to the accompaniment of a song pointed out by their companion, which depicted the graceful gestures of feet faltering with intoxication as sent by Vāsavadattā.
When the arrow is to be enacted, one should perform the mere gesture of displaying the lotus-turning,
while adopting a heroic gaze and relying solely upon the weapon.
With his eyes turned toward them and his mind captivated by curiosity,
the lord of men exclaimed with intense delight, "Oh, how charming is the play of these two graceful women!"

At the time of the pressure and friction of the hand, although I was being tormented while remaining upon the circle of the breast, you, on the other hand, having pulled me away, cast me somewhere else.

Not retreating from battle, proficiency in the arts of performance, delight in well-spoken words, application to interrogation, and family lore— these are the traditional sciences of princes.

Even deer, with ears pricked for the sound of song and mouths holding motionless mouthfuls of grass, sit motionless; such desirable things are indeed seized [by the senses].
He who, with a single blow, fells the boar that emerges from the heat of a forest fire and rushes headlong toward the thickets of the jungle, is worthy of worship.
Approaching silently without making a sound,
the excellent hunter effortlessly renders lifeless the hare sleeping within the thickets.
While Siṃhabhaṭa and his followers were thus boasting of their skill and agility in the sport of hunting,

How can the one whose weapon is the flower find a simultaneous resting place in her arched brows, her smiles, her glances, her soft words, her gestures, and her gait?
The destruction of Sunda and Upasunda was the fruit of the Self-born’s creation of Tilottamā;

Surrounded by *sumana* flowers, the braid of that woman— whose eyes were as tremulous as those of a young fawn— was like a long pond for embodied beings, serving as the cause for the fruit appropriate to their desires.

free from blemish, full of grace, and copper-hued from the intoxication of honey.
Even he who, devoted to asceticism, resorts to the slopes of the king of mountains to attain the bliss of union,

Her three-fold form— the division of her waist and the pair of arms joined with two hands—
produces even greater heat than that of the thousand-rayed sun, O gazelle-eyed one.
She is Sragdharā, she is Suvadanā, she is Prahārṣiṇī; she alone, she alone is Tanumadhyā. To whom does she not cause wonder? She is Rucirā, she is Mañjubhāṣiṇī. (DKuṭṭ 968)
